body: Which OOP concept allows a single interface to be used for different underlying data types?

options.whyWrong: Encapsulation is about bundling data with the methods that operate on it and restricting direct access.
Inheritance is about deriving one class from another; it enables but is not itself the "one interface, many types" idea.
Abstraction hides implementation detail behind a simpler model.

explanation: Polymorphism literally means "many forms" — the same call site dispatches to different implementations depending on the runtime type of the object.
concept: Compile-time polymorphism uses overloading; run-time polymorphism uses overriding through a base-class reference.

body: In Java, what is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?

options.body: Overloading resolves at compile time using the signature; overriding resolves at run time using the object type.
Overloading resolves at run time; overriding resolves at compile time.
options.whyWrong: The two are reversed — dynamic dispatch is what makes overriding a run-time mechanism.
Overriding must be resolved at run time because the actual object type is not known until then.

options.body: Overloading requires inheritance; overriding does not.
options.whyWrong: It is the other way round: overriding requires an inheritance relationship, overloading does not.

explanation: Overloading means several methods share a name but differ in parameter list; the compiler picks one from the static types. Overriding means a subclass replaces a superclass method with the same signature; the JVM picks the implementation from the object’s actual class at run time.
concept: Overloading = static/compile-time binding. Overriding = dynamic/run-time binding.

body: Which statement about abstract classes and interfaces (in modern Java) is correct?

options.body: A class can extend only one abstract class but implement many interfaces.
A class can extend many abstract classes but implement only one interface.
options.whyWrong: Java does not permit multiple class inheritance; the restriction applies to classes, not interfaces.

options.body: Interfaces cannot contain any method body at all.
options.whyWrong: Since Java 8 interfaces may contain default and static methods with bodies.
Abstract classes do have constructors, invoked via super() when a concrete subclass is instantiated.

explanation: Java allows single class inheritance but multiple interface implementation, which is how it avoids the classic diamond problem while still supporting multiple type contracts.

body: What does the Single Responsibility Principle state?

options.body: A class should have only one reason to change.
A class should have only one public method.
options.whyWrong: The principle is about reasons to change, not a method count.

options.body: A class should inherit from only one parent.
options.whyWrong: That describes single inheritance, a language rule rather than a design principle.

options.body: A method should take only one argument.
options.whyWrong: Argument count is a style concern, unrelated to SRP.

explanation: SRP says a class should have a single responsibility — equivalently, one axis of change. If two different stakeholders can force edits to the same class, it likely has two responsibilities.

options.whyWrong: The reference type is A, but instance methods dispatch on the object’s runtime type, which is B.
Assigning a subclass instance to a superclass reference is legal.
Only one method executes; the override replaces the base implementation.

explanation: The object is a B, and show() is overridden, so dynamic dispatch selects B.show(). The declared type A only limits which members you may call.
concept: Fields are resolved statically in Java; instance methods are resolved dynamically.

body: Which of these best describes composition over inheritance?

options.body: Prefer holding a reference to another object ("has-a") over deriving from it ("is-a") when you only need its behaviour.
Always avoid inheritance because it is deprecated in modern languages.
options.whyWrong: Inheritance is not deprecated; it is simply the wrong tool when there is no genuine is-a relationship.

options.body: Composition means combining two classes into one large class.
options.whyWrong: That is merging, not composition. Composition keeps the collaborator as a separate object.

options.body: Composition means making all fields public so other classes can reuse them.
options.whyWrong: That breaks encapsulation and is unrelated to composition.

explanation: Inheritance couples a subclass to its parent’s implementation. Composition delegates to a held object, which is easier to change, test and swap at run time.

body: A relation is in 2NF but has a transitive dependency A → B → C where A is the primary key. Which normal form does it violate?

options.whyWrong: 1NF only requires atomic values — a transitive dependency does not breach it.
The relation is stated to already be in 2NF, which forbids partial (not transitive) dependencies.
A 3NF violation is automatically a BCNF violation too, so 3NF is the tighter answer.

explanation: 3NF forbids a non-prime attribute being transitively dependent on the key. Here C depends on B, which depends on A, so C is transitively dependent on the key — a 3NF violation.
concept: 1NF: atomic values. 2NF: no partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF: no transitive dependency.

body: What does the "I" in ACID guarantee?

options.body: Concurrent transactions do not observe each other’s intermediate state.

options.whyWrong: That is Durability.

options.body: A transaction either completes fully or not at all.
options.whyWrong: That is Atomicity.

options.body: The database moves between valid states only.
options.whyWrong: That is Consistency.

explanation: Isolation means concurrently executing transactions are shielded from each other’s uncommitted changes, so the outcome is as if they ran in some serial order.

body: Which anomaly does a "dirty read" describe?

options.body: Reading data written by a transaction that has not yet committed.
Reading the same row twice and getting different values.
options.whyWrong: That is a non-repeatable read.

options.body: A query returning extra rows on re-execution.
options.whyWrong: That is a phantom read.

options.body: Two transactions waiting on each other forever.
options.whyWrong: That is a deadlock, not a read anomaly.

explanation: A dirty read exposes uncommitted changes. If the writer later rolls back, the reader has acted on data that never officially existed. READ COMMITTED and above prevent it.
concept: Isolation levels ascend: READ UNCOMMITTED → READ COMMITTED → REPEATABLE READ → SERIALIZABLE.

body: Which index structure is most appropriate for range queries such as "WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 80000"?

options.whyWrong: Hash indexes support equality lookups only; they do not preserve ordering, so ranges require a full scan.

options.body: Bitmap index on a high-cardinality column
options.whyWrong: Bitmap indexes suit low-cardinality columns and are not designed for numeric ranges.

options.body: No index — a full table scan is always faster
options.whyWrong: For a selective range a B+ tree scan of the leaf chain is typically far cheaper than a full scan.

explanation: B+ trees keep keys sorted and link leaf nodes, so a range query seeks once to the lower bound and then walks the leaves until the upper bound.

body: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique key?

options.body: A table has at most one primary key and it cannot be NULL; unique keys can be multiple and typically allow one NULL.
Both allow NULL values and there can be many of each.
options.whyWrong: A primary key can never be NULL and a table may have only one.

options.body: A unique key cannot be referenced by a foreign key.
options.whyWrong: Foreign keys may reference any uniquely constrained column, not just the primary key.

options.body: A primary key does not create an index.
options.whyWrong: Primary keys are backed by a unique index in every mainstream RDBMS.

explanation: Both enforce uniqueness. The primary key is the single chosen identifier for the row and is NOT NULL; additional unique constraints express alternate keys and generally permit a NULL.

body: A relation R(A, B, C, D) has functional dependencies AB → C and C → D. What is the highest normal form R satisfies (assuming AB is the only candidate key)?

options.whyWrong: D is transitively dependent on the key through C, which 3NF forbids.
BCNF is stricter than 3NF, and 3NF already fails here.
No non-prime attribute depends on part of AB alone, so 2NF is satisfied.

explanation: No attribute depends on just A or just B, so 2NF holds. But C → D with C non-prime creates a transitive dependency AB → C → D, breaking 3NF. The highest form satisfied is therefore 2NF.

body: Which join returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right, with NULLs where no match exists?

options.whyWrong: An inner join drops left rows that have no match.
That preserves the right table instead of the left.
A cross join produces the Cartesian product with no matching condition.

explanation: LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves every left-hand row, padding unmatched right-hand columns with NULL.

body: Given `employees(id, name, dept_id, salary)`, which query returns the second-highest salary?

options.body: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
SELECT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1;
options.whyWrong: This returns the highest salary, not the second highest.

options.body: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary <= (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
options.whyWrong: The `<=` includes the maximum itself, so this returns the highest salary again.

options.body: SELECT MIN(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT MIN(salary) FROM employees);
options.whyWrong: This finds the second-lowest salary.

explanation: Excluding the maximum with a strict `<` and then taking MAX of what remains yields the second-highest distinct salary. A window function (DENSE_RANK) is the modern alternative.
concept: Beware of ties: this pattern returns the second-highest distinct value.

body: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

options.body: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
They are interchangeable in all queries.
options.whyWrong: HAVING can reference aggregates; WHERE cannot, because aggregates are not yet computed.

options.body: HAVING filters rows before grouping; WHERE filters after.
options.whyWrong: The two are reversed.

options.body: WHERE works only on indexed columns.
options.whyWrong: WHERE works on any column; indexing only affects performance.

explanation: Logical processing order is FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. That is why HAVING can use COUNT(*) or SUM(...) but WHERE cannot.

body: How many rows does `SELECT COUNT(*)` versus `SELECT COUNT(col)` return differently when `col` contains NULLs?

options.body: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) skips rows where col IS NULL.

options.whyWrong: Aggregate functions other than COUNT(*) ignore NULL inputs.

options.body: COUNT(*) skips NULLs; COUNT(col) counts everything.
options.whyWrong: This is reversed.

options.body: COUNT(col) raises an error if col contains NULL.
options.whyWrong: NULLs are silently ignored, not an error.

explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(expression) counts non-NULL evaluations of that expression.

body: Which query lists each department with more than 5 employees, showing the department id and the count?

options.body: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 GROUP BY dept_id;
options.whyWrong: WHERE cannot reference an aggregate — it is evaluated before grouping.

options.body: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY COUNT(*) HAVING dept_id > 5;
options.whyWrong: Grouping by an aggregate is invalid, and the filter tests the wrong column.

options.body: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees ORDER BY COUNT(*) > 5;
options.whyWrong: ORDER BY sorts; it does not filter.

explanation: Group by the department, then filter the resulting groups with HAVING on the aggregate.

body: Which window function assigns 1, 2, 2, 4 to values ordered with a tie in second place?

options.whyWrong: DENSE_RANK would produce 1, 2, 2, 3 — it does not leave gaps after ties.
ROW_NUMBER always gives distinct 1, 2, 3, 4 and breaks ties arbitrarily.
NTILE distributes rows into buckets rather than ranking them.

explanation: RANK() gives tied rows the same rank and then skips ranks, producing the gap (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK closes the gap; ROW_NUMBER never ties.

body: What does `DELETE FROM employees;` do differently from `TRUNCATE TABLE employees;`?

options.body: DELETE removes rows one at a time and can be rolled back per row with triggers firing; TRUNCATE deallocates pages wholesale and usually does not fire row triggers.
They are identical in every respect.
options.whyWrong: They differ in logging, trigger behaviour, identity reset and typically in speed.

options.body: TRUNCATE can include a WHERE clause; DELETE cannot.
options.whyWrong: It is the reverse — DELETE accepts WHERE, TRUNCATE does not.

options.body: DELETE cannot be rolled back inside a transaction.
options.whyWrong: DELETE is fully transactional and can be rolled back.

explanation: DELETE is a DML row-by-row operation that logs each row and fires row triggers. TRUNCATE is closer to DDL: it drops storage in bulk, is much faster on large tables, and commonly resets identity counters.

body: Which scheduling algorithm can cause starvation of long jobs?

options.whyWrong: Round Robin gives every process a time slice, so no process waits indefinitely.
FCFS can cause the convoy effect but never indefinite starvation — every job eventually reaches the front.
Aging exists precisely to prevent starvation by promoting long-waiting processes.

explanation: SJF always prefers the shortest burst, so a steady arrival of short jobs can postpone a long job indefinitely. Aging is the standard remedy.

body: Which of the four Coffman conditions, if broken, prevents deadlock by allowing resources to be taken back?

options.whyWrong: Breaking mutual exclusion means sharing resources freely, which is unrelated to reclaiming them.
Breaking this means acquiring all resources up front, not taking them back.
Breaking this means imposing a global ordering on resource requests.

explanation: The four necessary conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait. Allowing preemption lets the OS forcibly reclaim a held resource, breaking the "no preemption" condition.

body: What is thrashing in an operating system?

options.body: The system spends more time servicing page faults than executing processes.
Two threads repeatedly acquire the same lock.
options.whyWrong: That is lock contention or livelock, not thrashing.

options.body: The CPU scheduler switches between processes too rarely.
options.whyWrong: Thrashing is about paging, not scheduling frequency.
That is fragmentation, a storage-layout problem.

explanation: When the combined working set exceeds physical memory, pages are evicted almost as soon as they are loaded. CPU utilisation collapses because processes are constantly blocked on page faults.
concept: The remedy is to reduce the degree of multiprogramming or add memory — a working-set model detects it.

body: What is the key difference between a process and a thread?

options.body: Threads of one process share its address space; separate processes have isolated address spaces.
Threads cannot run in parallel on multiple cores.
options.whyWrong: Threads are precisely the unit the kernel schedules onto cores.

options.body: A process cannot contain more than one thread.
options.whyWrong: Every process has at least one thread and may have many.

options.body: Processes are faster to create than threads.
options.whyWrong: Thread creation is cheaper because there is no new address space to build.

explanation: A process owns resources — address space, file descriptors — while threads are execution contexts inside it that share those resources but keep their own stack and registers.

body: Given page reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5 with 3 frames, how many page faults does FIFO incur?

options.whyWrong: Trace it again — none of the later references find their page still resident under FIFO.
Every one of the seven references misses; recheck the eviction order.
Far too few; only three frames are available for five distinct pages.

explanation: FIFO with 3 frames: 1(F)[1], 2(F)[1,2], 3(F)[1,2,3], 4(F evict 1)[2,3,4], 1(F evict 2)[3,4,1], 2(F evict 3)[4,1,2], 5(F evict 4)[1,2,5]. All seven references fault.
concept: This is the classic setup for Belady’s anomaly, where adding frames can increase FIFO faults.

body: A semaphore initialised to 1 and used with wait/signal around a critical section acts as:

options.body: A binary semaphore providing mutual exclusion
A counting semaphore allowing many concurrent entrants
options.whyWrong: A count of 1 permits only one entrant at a time.
Condition variables signal state changes and require an external lock.
Semaphore wait blocks the caller rather than spinning.

explanation: With an initial value of 1, at most one thread can pass wait() before another calls signal(), which is exactly mutual exclusion.

body: Which layer of the OSI model does a router primarily operate at?

options.whyWrong: Switches and bridges operate at Layer 2 using MAC addresses.
Layer 4 is where TCP and UDP live; routers forward on IP addresses.
Hubs and repeaters operate at Layer 1.

explanation: Routers forward packets using IP addresses and routing tables, which is Layer 3 — the network layer.

body: Which statement about TCP versus UDP is correct?

options.body: TCP guarantees ordered, reliable delivery with flow and congestion control; UDP does not.
UDP is connection-oriented and TCP is connectionless.
options.whyWrong: This is reversed — TCP establishes a connection via a handshake.

options.body: UDP guarantees ordering but not reliability.
options.whyWrong: UDP guarantees neither ordering nor delivery.

options.body: TCP has a smaller header than UDP.
options.whyWrong: TCP’s header is at least 20 bytes versus UDP’s 8.

explanation: TCP adds sequence numbers, acknowledgements, retransmission, flow control and congestion control. UDP is a thin datagram service, which is why latency-sensitive traffic often prefers it.

body: How many usable host addresses does a /26 IPv4 subnet provide?

options.whyWrong: That is the total address count; the network and broadcast addresses are not usable hosts.
That corresponds to a /27.
That corresponds to a /25.

explanation: A /26 leaves 6 host bits: 2⁶ = 64 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses, gives 62 usable hosts.
concept: Usable hosts = 2^(32 − prefix) − 2 for IPv4 subnets larger than /31.

body: What is the purpose of the TCP three-way handshake?

options.body: To synchronise initial sequence numbers and confirm both directions are reachable.

options.whyWrong: Encryption is TLS’s job, layered above TCP.

options.body: To negotiate the IP addresses of both hosts.
options.whyWrong: Addresses are already known before the handshake begins.
TCP does not perform compression.

explanation: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK lets each side advertise its initial sequence number and acknowledge the other’s, establishing a reliable bidirectional byte stream.

body: Which HTTP status code indicates that the client must authenticate to get the response?

options.whyWrong: 403 means the server understood who you are and still refuses — authentication will not help.
404 means the resource does not exist.
500 signals a server-side fault.

explanation: 401 means "unauthenticated" despite its name, and the response carries a WWW-Authenticate header. 403 means authenticated but not permitted.

body: What does DNS primarily do?

options.body: Resolve human-readable domain names to IP addresses.
Encrypt traffic between browser and server.
options.whyWrong: That is TLS.

options.body: Assign IP addresses to hosts joining a network.
options.whyWrong: That is DHCP.
That is BGP.

explanation: DNS is a distributed, hierarchical directory that maps names such as example.com to IP addresses.

options.body: The behaviour is unspecified — argument evaluation order is not defined in C

options.whyWrong: This assumes left-to-right evaluation, which the C standard does not guarantee.
Again this assumes a particular evaluation order.
This assumes an order the standard leaves open.

explanation: C does not specify the order in which function arguments are evaluated, and modifying x twice without an intervening sequence point is undefined behaviour. Different compilers legitimately print different results — this pattern should never appear in real code.
concept: Interview papers use this to test whether you recognise undefined behaviour rather than to test arithmetic.

body:
What does this pseudocode print?
```
SET a = 4
SET b = 0
WHILE a > 0 DO
    b = b + a
    a = a - 1
END WHILE
PRINT b
```

options.whyWrong: The loop accumulates every value from 4 down to 1, not just the first.
b is incremented on each of the four iterations.
That is 3 + 2 + 1 — the first iteration adds 4 as well.

explanation: The loop adds 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 and stops when a reaches 0.

body:
What is the time complexity of this pseudocode?
```
FOR i = 1 TO n DO
    j = 1
    WHILE j < n DO
        j = j * 2
    END WHILE
END FOR
```

options.whyWrong: The inner loop doubles j, so it runs log n times rather than n times.
The inner loop still contributes a log n factor for each of the n outer iterations.
This ignores the outer loop that runs n times.

explanation: The outer loop runs n times; the inner loop multiplies j by 2 until it reaches n, i.e. ⌈log₂ n⌉ iterations. Total: O(n log n).

body: In C, what does the expression `sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0])` compute for a locally declared array?

options.body: The number of elements in the array
The number of bytes in the array
options.whyWrong: That is sizeof(arr) alone, before dividing by the element size.

options.body: The index of the last element
options.whyWrong: The last index is one less than the element count.

options.body: Always 1, because arrays decay to pointers
options.whyWrong: Decay happens when an array is passed to a function, not where it is declared.

explanation: For an array still in scope as an array, sizeof gives its total byte size, so dividing by one element’s size yields the element count. Inside a function that received it as a pointer, this idiom silently breaks.

body: What is a memory leak?

options.body: Heap memory that is no longer reachable but was never released back to the allocator.
Reading past the end of an array.
options.whyWrong: That is a buffer overrun.

options.body: Dereferencing a pointer after the memory was freed.
options.whyWrong: That is a dangling-pointer or use-after-free bug.

options.body: Declaring more local variables than the stack can hold.
options.whyWrong: That is stack overflow.

explanation: A leak occurs when allocated memory becomes unreachable without being freed, so the process holds it until exit. Long-running services degrade as leaks accumulate.

body: Which statement about pass-by-value and pass-by-reference is correct?

options.body: Pass-by-value copies the argument, so the callee cannot change the caller’s variable itself.
Pass-by-value is impossible for objects in any language.
options.whyWrong: Many languages copy objects by value, and object *references* are themselves passed by value in Java.

options.body: Pass-by-reference always copies the whole object.
options.whyWrong: Passing by reference avoids the copy — that is its main purpose.
Java passes object *references* by value: reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller.

explanation: With pass-by-value the callee works on a copy, so assignments to the parameter are invisible to the caller. Java is strictly pass-by-value, though the value copied may be a reference — which is why mutating the pointed-to object is visible but reassigning is not.

body: What is the worst-case time complexity of QuickSort?

options.whyWrong: That is the average case; a pathological pivot choice degrades to quadratic.
No comparison sort can beat O(n log n), let alone reach O(log n).
Only non-comparison sorts such as counting sort achieve linear time.

explanation: If the pivot is always the smallest or largest element (for instance, the first element of an already-sorted array), each partition removes just one element, giving n levels of O(n) work — O(n²). Randomised or median-of-three pivots make this vanishingly unlikely.

body: Which data structure gives O(1) average-case insert, delete and lookup?

options.whyWrong: A balanced BST gives O(log n) for these operations.
Lookup is O(log n) and insertion is O(n) because of shifting.
A heap gives O(1) access to the minimum but O(log n) insert/delete and O(n) arbitrary lookup.

explanation: With a good hash function and bounded load factor, a hash table performs all three operations in O(1) expected time. Worst case degrades to O(n) when everything collides.

body: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits nodes in ascending key order?

options.whyWrong: Pre-order visits the root before its subtrees, so it does not produce sorted output.
Post-order visits the root last and is not sorted.
Level-order follows breadth-first layers, unrelated to key order.

explanation: In-order traversal (left, root, right) on a BST yields keys in ascending order — a common way to validate a BST.

body: What is the time complexity of building a heap from an unsorted array of n elements using the standard bottom-up heapify?

options.whyWrong: That is the cost of inserting elements one at a time; bottom-up heapify is asymptotically cheaper.
Every element must be examined at least once.
Far too slow — each node sifts down at most its height.

explanation: Most nodes sit near the bottom and sift down only a little. Summing height × node-count across levels converges to O(n), not O(n log n).
concept: Σ (n/2^(h+1)) × h over all heights h converges to 2n.

body: Which algorithm finds the shortest path in a weighted graph that may contain negative edge weights (but no negative cycles)?

options.whyWrong: Dijkstra assumes non-negative weights; a negative edge can invalidate an already-finalised distance.
BFS finds shortest paths only in unweighted graphs (or uniform weights).
Kruskal builds a minimum spanning tree, not shortest paths.

explanation: Bellman–Ford relaxes every edge V − 1 times, which tolerates negative weights and detects negative cycles with one extra pass. It costs O(V·E) versus Dijkstra’s O((V + E) log V).

body: Which traversal is used to produce a topological ordering of a DAG?

options.body: Depth-first search with reverse post-order (or Kahn’s in-degree algorithm)

options.whyWrong: Plain BFS from one node ignores in-degree constraints and may emit a node before its prerequisites.
In-order traversal is defined for binary trees, not general graphs.
Prim builds a minimum spanning tree on an undirected graph.

explanation: Pushing each node onto a stack after exploring all its descendants and then popping gives a valid topological order. Kahn’s algorithm achieves the same by repeatedly removing zero in-degree nodes.

body: What is the space complexity of the standard recursive merge sort on an array of n elements?

options.whyWrong: Standard merge sort needs an auxiliary buffer for merging; only sophisticated in-place variants approach O(1).
That is only the recursion-stack depth and ignores the merge buffer.
The buffer is reused across levels, so it does not multiply by the depth.

explanation: Merging needs a temporary array proportional to the range being merged, so O(n) auxiliary space dominates the O(log n) recursion stack.

body: Which problem is NOT naturally solved by dynamic programming?

options.whyWrong: LCS is a textbook DP with overlapping subproblems on prefix pairs.
Knapsack is the canonical DP over capacity and item index.
Edit distance is a standard two-dimensional DP.

explanation: MST is solved greedily (Kruskal or Prim) because the cut property guarantees a locally optimal edge is globally safe. It lacks the overlapping-subproblem structure DP exploits.

body: For a singly linked list, what is the time complexity of deleting a node given only a pointer to that node (not the head), assuming it is not the tail?

options.body: O(1) by copying the next node’s data and unlinking the next node
O(n) because you must find the previous node
options.whyWrong: The copy trick avoids needing the predecessor entirely.
It is possible for any non-tail node via the copy trick.
Linked lists offer no logarithmic access path.

explanation: Copy the successor’s value into the current node and then splice out the successor. This fails for the tail, since there is no successor to copy from.

body: Which data structure is best for implementing an LRU cache with O(1) get and put?

options.body: Hash map plus doubly linked list

options.whyWrong: Heap updates cost O(log n), so get and put are not O(1).
Maintaining sort order on access costs O(n) per operation.
A hash map alone cannot tell you which key is least recently used.

explanation: The hash map gives O(1) lookup to a list node; the doubly linked list gives O(1) unlink and move-to-front, so recency is maintained without scanning.

body: What is the minimum number of comparisons needed to find both the maximum and minimum of n elements?

options.whyWrong: That is the naive approach of two independent scans; pairing elements does better.
Sorting is unnecessary for finding just the extremes.
A single comparison per element cannot maintain both extremes.

explanation: Compare elements in pairs first (n/2 comparisons), then compare the smaller of each pair against the running minimum and the larger against the running maximum (n/2 each). Total ≈ 3n/2 − 2.

body: Binary search on a sorted array of 1,000,000 elements needs at most how many comparisons?

options.whyWrong: That is √n, the cost of jump search rather than binary search.
Recall that log₂(10⁶) ≈ 20.
That is linear search.

explanation: Binary search halves the range each step, needing ⌈log₂(10⁶)⌉ ≈ 20 comparisons.

body: Which of these is a stable sorting algorithm?

options.whyWrong: Standard in-place partitioning swaps distant elements and does not preserve the relative order of equal keys.
Heap sort’s sift operations reorder equal keys arbitrarily.
Selection sort swaps a minimum into place across the array, which can reorder equal keys.

explanation: Merge sort is stable when the merge step prefers the left run on ties. Stability matters when sorting by several keys in sequence.

body: A stack is used to check balanced parentheses. Which input causes the algorithm to report "unbalanced" only at the end of the scan?

options.whyWrong: The third character pops an empty stack, so the failure is detected mid-scan.
The mismatched closer is caught immediately when it appears.
This string is balanced.

explanation: Unmatched *openers* are only discovered when the scan ends and the stack is non-empty. Unmatched closers, by contrast, fail as soon as they are read.

body: What is the time complexity of finding whether a cycle exists in an undirected graph using DFS?

options.whyWrong: That is only true for an adjacency-matrix representation; with adjacency lists it is O(V + E).
That resembles Kruskal’s sorting cost, not a plain DFS.
That is Bellman–Ford territory.

explanation: DFS visits each vertex once and traverses each edge at most twice on adjacency lists, giving O(V + E).

body: What is the main purpose of a load balancer?

options.body: Distribute incoming requests across multiple servers and route around unhealthy ones.
Store frequently accessed data close to the client.
options.whyWrong: That is a cache or CDN.

options.body: Split a database table across multiple machines.
options.whyWrong: That is sharding.
Compression is a transport optimisation, not load balancing.

explanation: A load balancer spreads traffic across a pool of servers, performs health checks and enables horizontal scaling plus zero-downtime deploys.

body: Which caching strategy writes to the cache and the database at the same time?

options.whyWrong: Write-back updates the cache first and flushes to the database later, risking loss on failure.
Cache-aside has the application populate the cache only on a read miss.
Write-around bypasses the cache on writes entirely.

explanation: Write-through keeps cache and store consistent by writing both synchronously, at the cost of higher write latency.

body: In the CAP theorem, what must a distributed system sacrifice during a network partition?

options.whyWrong: Partitions are a fact of networks, not a property you can choose to drop.
Durability is an ACID property and is not part of CAP.
CAP states precisely that all three cannot hold simultaneously during a partition.

explanation: When the network partitions, a system either refuses requests to stay consistent (CP) or serves possibly stale data to stay available (AP). Partition tolerance is not optional in a real network.

body: Which HTTP method should be idempotent according to REST conventions?

options.whyWrong: POST typically creates a new resource each time, so repeating it has additional effects.
PATCH is not required to be idempotent — it depends on the patch semantics.
CONNECT establishes a tunnel and is not part of resource-manipulation semantics.

explanation: PUT replaces a resource with the supplied representation, so issuing it repeatedly leaves the same final state. GET, HEAD and DELETE are also idempotent; POST is not.

body: A recursive function computes fib(n) as fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) with no memoisation. Roughly how many calls does fib(30) make?

options.whyWrong: That is the number of leaves in a full binary tree of depth 30, but the recursion tree is not full — it is skewed by the n-2 branch.
That is the depth of the recursion, not the number of calls.
Quadratic growth would describe a memoised or iterative version, not the naive one.

explanation: The call count follows the Fibonacci numbers themselves, which grow like φ^n where φ ≈ 1.618. So fib(30) makes on the order of 1.6^30 calls — a few million — which is why the naive version becomes unusable around n = 40.
concept: A recursion that recomputes the same subproblems has a cost equal to the size of its recursion tree, not its depth.
hint: How many nodes are in the recursion tree, not how deep is it?

body: What is the maximum depth of the call stack when quicksort is implemented recursively on an already-sorted array of n elements, always picking the last element as pivot?

options.whyWrong: log n depth applies when the pivot splits the array evenly — this is the worst case, not the best.
That is quicksort’s average time complexity, not its stack depth.
The recursion does not stop after two levels; each call recurses on n-1 elements.

explanation: With a last-element pivot on sorted input, every partition puts n-1 elements on one side and none on the other. The recursion therefore descends one element at a time, giving a stack depth of n — which is how quicksort causes stack overflow on large sorted inputs.
concept: Quicksort’s stack depth mirrors its partition balance: even splits give log n, degenerate splits give n.
hint: What does the partition look like when the input is already in order?

body: In backtracking, what does "pruning" mean?

options.body: Abandoning a partial candidate as soon as it cannot possibly extend to a valid solution
Removing duplicate solutions after the search finishes
options.whyWrong: Deduplicating results afterwards does not reduce the work already done; pruning is about avoiding that work.

options.body: Limiting the recursion to a fixed depth
options.whyWrong: A depth cap is a different technique and can miss valid solutions; pruning never discards a branch that could succeed.
Sorting can help pruning be more effective, but it is not itself pruning.

explanation: Pruning cuts a branch of the search tree the moment the partial candidate violates a constraint — for example abandoning an N-Queens placement as soon as two queens attack each other, rather than completing the board and then checking. The saving is the entire subtree below that point.
concept: Backtracking is depth-first search over partial candidates; pruning is what makes it tractable.
hint: What happens to the whole subtree below a branch you abandon?

body: A recursive solution to the subset-sum problem explores every subset of n items. What is its time complexity without pruning or memoisation?

options.whyWrong: Quadratic would only cover pairs of items, not every combination.
That is the cost of sorting, which does not enumerate subsets.
Factorial counts orderings; subsets are unordered, so each item is simply in or out.

explanation: Each of the n items is either included or excluded, giving 2^n subsets, and the recursion visits each one. Note that the pseudo-polynomial dynamic-programming solution is O(n × target), which is much faster when the target is small.
concept: Include-or-exclude recursion over n items is 2^n; permutation recursion is n!.
hint: How many independent binary choices are there?

body: Which of these is the base case that a recursive function must have to terminate?

options.body: A condition under which it returns without calling itself
A call to itself with a smaller argument
options.whyWrong: That is the recursive step. Without a base case it would recurse forever.

options.body: A loop that runs a fixed number of times
options.whyWrong: A loop inside the function does not stop the recursion from continuing.

options.body: A try/catch around the recursive call
options.whyWrong: Catching the resulting stack overflow is not termination; the function still never completes normally.

explanation: Every recursion needs at least one input for which it returns an answer directly, without recursing. The recursive step must also move strictly towards that case — a base case that is never reached is as broken as not having one.
concept: Termination needs both a base case and progress towards it.
hint: What has to be true for the chain of calls to ever stop?

body: Converting a recursive function into an iterative one usually requires an explicit what?

options.whyWrong: A queue gives breadth-first order; recursion is inherently depth-first, which is what a stack models.
A hash map may memoise results but does not replace the call structure.
A heap orders by priority, which is unrelated to the order recursive calls return in.

explanation: Recursion is implemented by the machine’s call stack, which stores each pending frame. Rewriting it iteratively means maintaining that stack yourself — which is exactly what an iterative depth-first traversal does.
concept: The call stack is the data structure recursion uses; making it explicit is what converts recursion to iteration.
hint: What does the machine already use to track pending calls?

body: What does the expression n & (n - 1) do?

options.body: Clears the lowest set bit of n
Sets the lowest zero bit of n
options.whyWrong: That is n | (n + 1). The AND with n-1 can only clear bits, never set them.
Bit reversal cannot be done with a single AND.
Halving is n >> 1. For n = 12 (1100), n & (n-1) is 8, not 6.

explanation: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and turns every bit below it into 1. ANDing with n therefore keeps all higher bits and clears that lowest set bit: 12 (1100) & 11 (1011) = 8 (1000). Repeating this counts set bits in as many steps as there are ones.
concept: n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit; n & -n isolates it.
hint: Write 12 and 11 in binary and AND them.

body: How can you test whether a positive integer n is a power of two using a single bitwise expression?

options.whyWrong: OR-ing sets bits rather than clearing them, so this is zero only when n is zero.
XOR of n and n-1 is never zero for positive n, because they differ in at least one bit.
That is true only for n = 1, not for 2, 4, 8 and so on.

explanation: A power of two has exactly one set bit, and n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit — so the result is zero precisely when there was only one bit to clear. Guard for n = 0 separately, since 0 & -1 is also 0 but 0 is not a power of two.
concept: Exactly-one-set-bit is the defining property of a power of two.
hint: What does clearing the only set bit leave you with?

body: In an array where every number appears twice except one, which single operation finds the unique number in O(n) time and O(1) space?

options.whyWrong: Summing needs the pairs to cancel, which they do not — and it can overflow.
AND collapses towards zero and loses the information about which value was unpaired.
OR accumulates set bits from every element, so the duplicates do not cancel.

explanation: XOR is its own inverse (x ^ x = 0) and is commutative, so every duplicated pair cancels to zero and the survivor is XORed with 0, leaving itself. It needs one pass and one accumulator.
concept: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x — the two identities that make XOR cancel duplicates.
hint: Which operation makes a value cancel itself out?

body: What is the value of 5 << 2?

options.whyWrong: That is 5 << 1. Shifting left by 2 multiplies by 4, not 2.
Shifting is not addition; 5 + 2 is not what << computes.
Shifting is not exponentiation either.

explanation: A left shift by k multiplies by 2^k, so 5 << 2 = 5 × 4 = 20. In binary, 101 becomes 10100.
concept: x << k is x × 2^k; x >> k is floor division by 2^k for non-negative x.
hint: Write 5 in binary and move every bit two places left.

body: Why is x >> 1 not always the same as x / 2 in a language like Java or C?

options.body: They round differently for negative numbers

options.whyWrong: Shifting is typically at least as fast; speed is not the difference in behaviour.
A right shift moves towards zero magnitude and cannot overflow.

options.body: They differ for odd numbers only when positive
options.whyWrong: For positive odd numbers both give the same floor result — the divergence is on the negative side.

explanation: Arithmetic right shift rounds towards negative infinity, while integer division rounds towards zero. For x = -7: -7 >> 1 is -4, but -7 / 2 is -3. For non-negative values the two agree.
concept: Shift rounds towards −∞; integer division truncates towards 0.
hint: Try it with −7.

body: How do you set the k-th bit of an integer n (counting from 0)?

options.whyWrong: That tests the bit rather than setting it, and clears everything else.
XOR toggles the bit — it clears it if it was already set.
That clears the k-th bit rather than setting it.

explanation: 1 << k is a mask with only the k-th bit set. OR-ing leaves every other bit untouched and forces that one to 1, whether or not it already was. The companion operations are & ~mask to clear and ^ mask to toggle.
concept: OR to set, AND-NOT to clear, XOR to toggle, AND to test.
hint: Which operator can only ever turn bits on?

body: Which problem is correctly solved by a greedy algorithm?

options.body: Selecting the maximum number of non-overlapping activities by earliest finish time
0/1 knapsack with arbitrary weights and values
options.whyWrong: Greedy by value-to-weight ratio can be beaten here; 0/1 knapsack needs dynamic programming.

options.body: Finding the longest path in a general graph
options.whyWrong: Longest path is NP-hard and no greedy rule solves it.

options.body: Counting the number of distinct subsets summing to a target
options.whyWrong: Counting requires exploring combinations, which a single greedy pass cannot do.

explanation: Activity selection has the greedy-choice property: repeatedly taking the activity that finishes earliest always leaves the most room for the rest, and this can be proved by an exchange argument. Fractional knapsack is also greedy; the 0/1 version is not.
concept: Greedy is correct only when a local optimum provably leads to a global one — usually shown by an exchange argument.
hint: Which of these has a provable exchange argument?

body: Why does the greedy coin-change algorithm (always take the largest coin that fits) fail for some coin systems?

options.body: A large coin can force more small coins than a different combination would need
It is too slow for large amounts
options.whyWrong: Greedy coin change is fast; correctness, not speed, is the problem.

options.body: It cannot handle amounts larger than the biggest coin
options.whyWrong: It handles those fine by taking the big coin repeatedly.

options.body: It requires the coins to be sorted
options.whyWrong: Sorting is trivial and is not why the result can be wrong.

explanation: With coins {1, 3, 4} and a target of 6, greedy takes 4 then 1 then 1 — three coins — while 3 + 3 uses two. The greedy choice is only safe for canonical systems such as Indian or US denominations; in general the problem needs dynamic programming.
concept: A greedy rule that works on one input set can be wrong on another — correctness has to be proved, not assumed from examples.
hint: Try coins {1, 3, 4} and a target of 6.

body: Huffman coding builds its tree by repeatedly combining which two nodes?

options.body: The two with the smallest frequencies
The two with the largest frequencies
options.whyWrong: Combining the largest first would push frequent symbols deeper, producing longer codes for common characters.

options.body: The two that are alphabetically adjacent
options.whyWrong: Huffman ignores symbol order entirely; only frequency matters.

options.body: A random pair, since the result is the same either way
options.whyWrong: The pairing rule is what makes the code optimal; a random pair does not.

explanation: Taking the two least frequent nodes each time pushes rare symbols deepest in the tree, so they receive the longest codes and frequent symbols the shortest. That is the greedy choice, and it provably yields a minimum weighted path length.
concept: Huffman is the standard example of a greedy algorithm with a proof of optimality.
hint: Which symbols should end up with the longest codes?

body: What is the time complexity of inserting an element at the beginning of a dynamic array of n elements?

options.whyWrong: Only appending at the end is amortised O(1); inserting at the front must move everything.
Logarithmic cost implies halving the work each step, which shifting does not do.
That is sorting cost, not a single insertion.

explanation: Every existing element has to shift one position right to make room, so the cost is proportional to n. A linked list or a deque gives O(1) insertion at the front instead.
concept: Arrays are cheap at the end and expensive at the front; linked lists are the reverse.
hint: What has to move to make space?

body: You need to find whether any value repeats in an unsorted array of n integers. Which approach is fastest on average?

options.body: Insert into a hash set and stop on the first repeat

options.whyWrong: That works but costs O(n²), far more than a single pass with a set.

options.body: Sort, then scan for adjacent equals
options.whyWrong: Correct, but O(n log n) — slower than the hash approach and it mutates the array.
Binary search needs sorted input, and searching for an element you are iterating over finds itself.

explanation: One pass adding each value to a hash set, checking membership first, is O(n) on average and O(n) space. The sorting approach is a good answer when you must not use extra space.
concept: Trading memory for time with a hash set is the standard first move on duplicate problems.
hint: What lets you check "have I seen this?" in constant time?

body: Kadane’s algorithm finds the maximum subarray sum in O(n). What does it track at each position?

options.body: The best sum ending exactly at this index, and the best seen anywhere
The running total of the whole array
options.whyWrong: A plain running total cannot recover from a long negative stretch.

options.body: The largest single element so far
options.whyWrong: That only helps when every element is negative; it ignores contiguous sums.

options.body: A sorted list of all prefix sums
options.whyWrong: Kadane keeps two numbers, not a list — that is what makes it O(1) space.

explanation: At each index Kadane decides whether to extend the previous subarray or start fresh: best_ending_here = max(x, best_ending_here + x). The overall answer is the maximum of that quantity across all positions.
concept: Many linear-scan DP problems reduce to "best ending here" plus "best overall".
hint: What two numbers are enough to carry forward?

body: Two pointers moving towards each other from the ends of a sorted array is the standard technique for which problem?

options.body: Finding a pair that sums to a target
Finding the median of two sorted arrays
options.whyWrong: That needs a partition-based binary search, not a simple converging scan.
Cycle detection uses two pointers at different speeds in a linked structure, not converging ends.
Two converging pointers can reverse an array, but that does not require the array to be sorted.

explanation: Because the array is sorted, a sum that is too small can only be increased by moving the left pointer right, and one that is too large by moving the right pointer left. Each step eliminates a candidate, giving O(n) with no extra space.
concept: Sorted input plus converging pointers turns many O(n²) pair searches into O(n).
hint: Why does sorting make one direction obviously right?

body: What does the sliding-window technique require of the problem to work correctly?

options.body: That extending or shrinking the window updates the answer in O(1)

options.whyWrong: Sliding windows work on unsorted arrays; substring and subarray problems rarely sort first.
Positivity matters for some variable-size window problems but is not a general requirement.

options.body: That the window size is fixed in advance
options.whyWrong: Variable-size windows are common — the longest-substring problems grow and shrink.

explanation: A window is only cheaper than recomputing if adding the incoming element and removing the outgoing one can each be done in constant time, usually with a running sum or a frequency map. Without that the technique degenerates to the brute force it replaced.
concept: Sliding windows trade recomputation for incremental update.
hint: What makes moving the window cheaper than recomputing it?

body: Given an array of n+1 integers where each value is between 1 and n, why must there be at least one duplicate?

options.whyWrong: Order has nothing to do with it; a sorted array of the same values has the same duplicate.
n+1 is not always even, and parity is irrelevant.

options.body: Only if the values are randomly chosen
options.whyWrong: It holds for every possible arrangement, random or not.

explanation: There are n+1 values drawn from only n distinct possibilities, so at least two must land on the same value. This is what guarantees Floyd’s cycle-detection solution to the find-the-duplicate problem always terminates.
concept: Pigeonhole turns "there might be a duplicate" into "there must be".
hint: How many slots, and how many items?

body: What is the amortised cost of appending to a dynamic array that doubles its capacity when full?

options.whyWrong: Only the appends that trigger a resize cost O(n); the rest are constant.
Doubling happens log n times in total, but the cost is spread across n appends, not paid per append.
That is the total cost of sorting n items, not of building an array.

explanation: Copying happens on the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 8th … append, so the total copying work across n appends is 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n < 2n. Divided over n appends that is a constant amortised cost, even though individual appends occasionally cost O(n).
concept: Amortised analysis averages an expensive-but-rare operation across the cheap ones.
hint: Add up the cost of all the resizes, then divide by n.

body: Rotating an array left by k positions in O(1) extra space is usually done by how many reversals?

options.whyWrong: A single reversal reverses the whole array, which is not a rotation.
Two reversals get the halves right but leave the array reversed overall.
Rotating one position k times is O(nk), which defeats the point.

explanation: Reverse the first k elements, reverse the remaining n−k, then reverse the whole array. Each element ends up shifted by exactly k, in O(n) time and O(1) space.
concept: The reversal trick converts rotation into three linear passes with no extra buffer.
hint: Try it by hand on [1,2,3,4,5] with k = 2.

body: Prefix sums let you answer a range-sum query on a static array in what time, after preprocessing?

options.whyWrong: Scanning the range is exactly what the prefix array exists to avoid.
Logarithmic query time is what a Fenwick or segment tree gives when updates are also needed.
That is a preprocessing cost, not a query cost.

explanation: With prefix[i] holding the sum of the first i elements, the sum of the range [l, r] is prefix[r+1] − prefix[l] — one subtraction. Preprocessing is O(n); the technique only applies while the array does not change.
concept: Prefix sums are the standard answer for many range queries on immutable data.
hint: What single arithmetic operation recovers a range from two prefixes?

body: Which statement about arrays and cache performance is true?

options.body: Sequential access is faster than random access because of spatial locality
Access time is identical regardless of order, since indexing is O(1)
options.whyWrong: O(1) describes the instruction count, not the memory latency, which varies hugely with cache hits.

options.body: Arrays have worse locality than linked lists
options.whyWrong: Arrays are contiguous, which is exactly what gives them better locality than a scattered linked list.

options.body: Cache behaviour only matters for arrays larger than main memory
options.whyWrong: It matters as soon as the working set exceeds a cache level, long before RAM is exhausted.

explanation: A cache line holds several adjacent elements, so walking an array in order gets many of them for one memory fetch. This is why an O(n²) algorithm over a contiguous array sometimes beats an O(n log n) one over pointers in practice.
concept: Big-O counts operations; real running time also depends on memory layout.
hint: What does the hardware fetch when you read one element?

body: Why is repeated string concatenation in a loop O(n²) in Java or Python?

options.body: Strings are immutable, so each concatenation copies the whole accumulated result

options.whyWrong: A single loop over n items is linear; the cost comes from what happens inside it.
Comparison is not involved in concatenation.

options.body: Garbage collection runs on every iteration
options.whyWrong: GC timing is unpredictable and is not what makes the asymptotic cost quadratic.

explanation: Each concatenation allocates a new string and copies everything built so far, so the copies total 1 + 2 + … + n ≈ n²/2 characters. Using a StringBuilder or collecting into a list and joining once brings it back to O(n).
concept: Immutability turns "append" into "copy everything", which is why builders exist.
hint: What happens to the existing characters on each step?

body: Checking whether two strings are anagrams is most efficiently done by which method?

options.body: Counting character frequencies in one pass over each

options.whyWrong: Correct, but O(n log n) versus O(n) for counting.
Different strings can share a hash code, and equal hashes do not imply an anagram.

options.body: Generating all permutations of one and searching
options.whyWrong: That is factorial time and hopeless for anything but tiny inputs.

explanation: Build a frequency map (or a fixed 26-slot array for lowercase letters) for the first string, decrement it walking the second, and check every count is zero. That is O(n) time and O(1) space for a fixed alphabet.
concept: Frequency counting beats sorting whenever only the multiset of characters matters.
hint: Do you need the order, or just the counts?

body: What is the worst-case time complexity of naive substring search (checking every starting position)?

options.whyWrong: That is what KMP achieves by reusing partial match information; the naive version does not.
No divide-and-conquer step is involved in the naive scan.
The cost depends on both the text length n and pattern length m, not m alone.

explanation: With text length n and pattern length m, there are about n starting positions and each can compare up to m characters before failing — for example searching "aaab" inside "aaaaaaaa". KMP avoids the re-comparison and runs in O(n + m).
concept: The naive scan re-examines characters it has already matched; KMP’s prefix table is what removes that waste.
hint: What input makes every starting position fail only at the last character?

body: A palindrome check using two pointers from both ends runs in what time and space?

options.whyWrong: Reversing into a new string would cost O(n) space; the two-pointer version needs none.

options.body: O(n log n) time, O(1) space
options.whyWrong: No sorting or halving is involved.
Each character is visited once, not once per position.

explanation: The pointers move towards each other comparing one pair per step, touching each character at most once and storing only two indices. Reversing the string and comparing is also O(n) time but uses O(n) extra space.
concept: Two converging pointers is the O(1)-space alternative to building a reversed copy.
hint: Do you need a second copy of the string?

body: In the sliding-window solution to "longest substring without repeating characters", when does the left pointer move?

options.body: When the incoming character is already inside the window

options.whyWrong: Moving it every step would keep the window a fixed size and miss longer answers.

options.body: Only when the window reaches a fixed maximum length
options.whyWrong: There is no fixed maximum; the answer is whatever the longest valid window turns out to be.

options.body: When the incoming character is a letter rather than a digit
options.whyWrong: Character class is irrelevant — only repetition matters.

explanation: The window must always hold distinct characters, so when a duplicate arrives the left edge advances past the previous occurrence of that character, restoring the invariant. Each pointer moves forward at most n times, giving O(n) overall.
concept: Sliding-window problems are defined by the invariant the window maintains.
hint: What property must the window always satisfy?

body: Which data structure gives the most efficient prefix search over a large dictionary of words?

options.whyWrong: A hash map finds exact keys in O(1) but cannot enumerate everything sharing a prefix without scanning all keys.
A BST can range-scan a prefix but compares whole strings at each node, costing more than walking a trie.
A heap orders by priority and offers no prefix structure at all.

explanation: A trie stores one character per edge, so following a prefix of length p costs O(p) regardless of dictionary size, and the subtree below that point contains exactly the words sharing the prefix. This is what powers autocomplete.
concept: Tries trade memory for prefix-structured lookup.
hint: Which structure shares storage between words with the same beginning?

body: What does it mean for a string comparison to be "lexicographic"?

options.body: Characters are compared position by position, and the first difference decides

options.whyWrong: Length only decides when one string is a prefix of the other; "b" comes after "ab".

options.body: Strings are compared by their total character-code sum
options.whyWrong: Summing loses position information — "ab" and "ba" would compare equal.
That depends on the encoding; in ASCII uppercase actually comes first.

explanation: Comparison walks both strings together and returns as soon as the characters differ. If one string runs out first and everything matched so far, the shorter one is smaller — which is why "app" sorts before "apple".
concept: Lexicographic order is dictionary order generalised to any character set.
hint: What decides the result — the first difference, or the whole string?

body: Why can string reversal be wrong if you reverse the underlying bytes of a UTF-8 string?

options.body: A character can occupy several bytes, and reversing bytes splits it apart
UTF-8 strings cannot be reversed at all
options.whyWrong: They can be reversed correctly — by code point or grapheme cluster rather than by byte.
Reversal is linear whichever unit you iterate over.

options.body: UTF-8 stores characters in reverse order already
options.whyWrong: It does not; UTF-8 is a straightforward variable-length encoding in reading order.

explanation: In UTF-8 an ASCII character is one byte but many others take two to four. Reversing the byte sequence produces invalid sequences in the middle of multi-byte characters. Correct reversal iterates code points — and for emoji or combining accents, grapheme clusters.
concept: Byte length, character count and display width are three different things.
hint: What is the smallest unit that is safe to reorder?

body: Binary search requires the array to be what?

options.whyWrong: Duplicates are fine; the search still finds a matching element.
Length parity is irrelevant to the halving step.
Contiguity helps performance but binary search also works over any random-access sequence.

explanation: Each step discards half the range based on a comparison with the middle element, which is only valid if everything to one side is smaller and everything to the other is larger. On unsorted input the discarded half may contain the target.
concept: Binary search trades a sortedness precondition for logarithmic lookup.
hint: Why is it safe to throw away half the array?

body: Why is `mid = low + (high - low) / 2` preferred over `mid = (low + high) / 2`?

options.body: It avoids integer overflow when low and high are both large

options.whyWrong: Both forms cost the same handful of instructions.
Neither form helps with unsorted input.
Both use integer arithmetic; neither yields a fraction.

explanation: For large indices low + high can exceed the maximum signed integer and wrap negative, producing an out-of-bounds index. Subtracting first keeps the intermediate value within range. This was a real bug in Java’s binary search for nearly a decade.
concept: Intermediate values can overflow even when both operands and the result are in range.
hint: What is the largest value low + high can reach?

body: Binary search on a rotated sorted array works because at every step which invariant holds?

options.body: At least one of the two halves is itself sorted
The array is still fully sorted
options.whyWrong: Rotation breaks global sortedness — that is what makes the problem non-trivial.

options.body: The target is always in the left half
options.whyWrong: There is no such guarantee; deciding which half to keep is the whole problem.

options.body: The rotation point is always at the middle
options.whyWrong: The rotation point can be anywhere.

explanation: Cutting a rotated sorted array at any midpoint leaves one side without the rotation point, so that side is in order. Comparing the target against that sorted side tells you which half to keep, preserving O(log n).
concept: Rotation preserves local sortedness even though global order is lost.
hint: If the break point is on one side, what does that make the other side?

body: "Binary search on the answer" is used when what is true?

options.body: The feasibility of a candidate answer is monotonic — if x works, everything above (or below) it works too
The input array is already sorted
options.whyWrong: The technique searches a range of possible answers, not the input, which need not be sorted.

options.body: The answer is guaranteed to be a power of two
options.whyWrong: No such restriction exists.

options.body: The problem has no greedy solution
options.whyWrong: Many problems solved this way also have greedy checkers; the two are complementary.

explanation: You binary-search the space of answers rather than the data, using a predicate that says whether a candidate is achievable. It is valid only when that predicate is monotonic — as in "can we split the array into k parts each summing to at most X?", where a larger X is always at least as easy.
concept: If a yes/no check is monotonic in the parameter, you can binary-search the parameter.
hint: What has to be true about the check as the candidate grows?

body: Searching a hash table has what worst-case time complexity?

options.whyWrong: That is the average case; the worst case is different.
Logarithmic lookup describes balanced trees, not hash tables.
No sorting occurs during a lookup.

explanation: If every key hashes to the same bucket, lookup degenerates to scanning a single chain of n entries. Average O(1) assumes a good hash function and a bounded load factor — which is why hash flooding is a real denial-of-service vector.
concept: Average and worst case differ sharply for hashing; the average depends on assumptions about the keys.

body: Interpolation search can beat binary search on which kind of data?

options.body: Sorted data that is close to uniformly distributed

options.whyWrong: On skewed data interpolation search can degrade to O(n), worse than binary search’s guaranteed O(log n).

options.whyWrong: Both need random access to a middle element, which a linked list does not provide.

explanation: Instead of always probing the midpoint, interpolation search estimates the position from the value, giving O(log log n) on uniform data. The estimate is only good when values are spread evenly; on clustered data it can probe almost linearly.
concept: Interpolation search trades a worst-case guarantee for a better average on well-behaved data.
hint: What assumption does estimating the position require?

body: Which sorting algorithm is stable?

options.whyWrong: Standard in-place quicksort swaps distant elements and is not stable.
Heapsort’s sift operations reorder equal elements arbitrarily.
Selection sort swaps the minimum into place, which can jump an equal element over another.

explanation: A stable sort preserves the relative order of records comparing equal — essential when sorting by one key after another. Merge sort achieves it by taking from the left run on ties.
concept: Stability matters whenever you sort by a secondary key first and a primary key second.
hint: Which algorithm can break ties consistently by construction?

body: Counting sort runs in O(n + k). What is k, and when does that make it a bad choice?

options.body: The range of input values — it is poor when the range is far larger than n
The number of comparisons — it is poor on large arrays
options.whyWrong: Counting sort makes no comparisons at all; that is why it beats the n log n bound.

options.body: The number of buckets you choose — it is poor if you pick too few
options.whyWrong: The bucket count is determined by the value range, not chosen freely.

options.whyWrong: Counting sort is not recursive and is indifferent to existing order.

explanation: Counting sort allocates one counter per possible value, so sorting a hundred integers spread over a billion possible values would allocate a billion counters. It shines when the range is small and known — ages, exam scores, byte values.

hint: What does the algorithm allocate before it starts counting?

body: Why is the lower bound for comparison-based sorting Ω(n log n)?

options.body: There are n! possible orderings and each comparison distinguishes at most two branches
Because merge sort is O(n log n)
options.whyWrong: A single algorithm’s cost is an upper bound, not proof that nothing can be faster.

concept: Information-theoretic lower bounds count how much a single operation can reveal.
hint: How many outcomes must the algorithm tell apart?

body: On nearly sorted data, which algorithm performs best?

options.whyWrong: That is quicksort’s worst case on sorted input, degrading to O(n²).
Heapsort is O(n log n) regardless of existing order and gains nothing from it.
Selection sort always scans the whole remaining array, so it is O(n²) whatever the input.

explanation: Insertion sort costs O(n + d) where d is the number of inversions, approaching linear when the data is nearly ordered. This is why real library sorts switch to insertion sort for small or nearly-sorted runs — Timsort is built on the idea.
concept: Adaptive algorithms exploit existing order; non-adaptive ones ignore it.
hint: Which algorithm does almost no work when every element is already near its place?

body: What makes quicksort’s average case O(n log n) despite an O(n²) worst case?

options.body: A random or median-of-three pivot makes badly unbalanced partitions very unlikely
The worst case cannot actually occur
options.whyWrong: It occurs readily with a fixed pivot on sorted input — a common real-world bug.
Partitioning scans the whole range and is O(n).

options.body: It uses extra memory to balance the partitions
options.whyWrong: Quicksort partitions in place; it uses no balancing buffer.

explanation: Each partition costs O(n), so the total is O(n × depth). A reasonable pivot keeps the expected depth at O(log n). Randomising the pivot means no fixed input can reliably trigger the quadratic case.
concept: Randomisation converts a bad worst case into an unlikely one.
hint: What determines the depth of the recursion?

body: What is the height of a balanced binary search tree containing n nodes?

options.whyWrong: That is the height of a degenerate tree that has become a linked list.
Height cannot exceed n; n log n is a time complexity, not a height.
A constant height would mean the tree holds a bounded number of nodes.

explanation: Balancing keeps each subtree’s size within a constant factor of its sibling, so the node count roughly doubles per level and the depth grows logarithmically. This is what guarantees O(log n) search, insert and delete.
concept: A BST’s operations are O(height); balancing is what keeps the height logarithmic.
hint: How many nodes fit in a tree of depth d?

body: An in-order traversal of a binary search tree produces the values in what order?

options.whyWrong: Insertion order is not recoverable from the tree structure.

options.whyWrong: That is a breadth-first traversal, not in-order.
Reversing the traversal gives descending; plain in-order gives ascending.

explanation: In-order visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. Since a BST keeps smaller values left and larger right, this yields sorted output — which is how you validate a BST in linear time.
concept: In-order traversal of a BST is a sorted scan.
hint: Where do the smaller values live?

body: Which traversal would you use to delete every node of a tree safely?

options.whyWrong: Freeing a node before its children leaves you without the pointers needed to reach them.
In-order frees the left subtree, then the node — losing the pointer to the right subtree.
Level-order works if you queue children before freeing, but post-order is the natural recursive answer.

explanation: Post-order visits both children before the node itself, so a node is only freed once nothing still needs its pointers. The same ordering is why post-order is used to compute a value that depends on both subtrees, such as height.
concept: Post-order is the traversal for anything that must handle children before the parent.
hint: When is it safe to free a node?

body: What is the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height h?

options.whyWrong: That is the maximum number of nodes, which is a perfectly full tree.

No recurrence in AVL analysis produces a quadratic bound.

concept: The sparsest allowed shape is what bounds a balanced tree’s height.
hint: What is the most unbalanced an AVL node is allowed to be?

body: In a binary search tree, deleting a node with two children is usually handled how?

options.body: Replace it with its in-order successor or predecessor

options.whyWrong: Promoting one child leaves the other subtree unattached.
That would discard values that should remain in the tree.

options.body: Mark it deleted and leave it in place
options.whyWrong: Tombstoning is a valid engineering choice but is not the standard BST deletion algorithm.

explanation: The in-order successor is the smallest value in the right subtree, so it is larger than everything left and smaller than everything else right — exactly the ordering property the removed node had. It has at most one child, so removing it from its old position is the easy case.
concept: BST deletion reduces the hard case to an easier one by substituting a boundary value.
hint: Which value could sit in that position without breaking the ordering?

body: Validating that a binary tree is a BST by only comparing each node with its two children is wrong. Why?

options.body: A node deeper in a subtree can violate an ancestor’s bound while satisfying its parent

options.whyWrong: Cost is not the issue; the check gives wrong answers.

options.body: Because the tree may be unbalanced
options.whyWrong: Balance and BST validity are independent properties.

explanation: Consider root 10 with left child 5 and that node’s right child 20. Every parent-child pair looks fine, but 20 sits in the left subtree of 10 and breaks the invariant. The correct check carries a (min, max) range down the recursion.
concept: A BST invariant is about whole subtrees, not adjacent pairs.
hint: Can a node be bigger than its parent but still be in the wrong subtree?

body: A complete binary tree with n nodes is usually stored in an array. Where is the left child of index i?

options.whyWrong: That is the next node in level order, which is the sibling or a cousin, not the child.
That is the parent, not the child.
That formula is off by one and would point above the node for small i.

explanation: With 0-based indexing the children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2 and the parent is ⌊(i−1)/2⌋. The array layout works precisely because a complete tree has no gaps — which is why binary heaps use it and need no pointers.
concept: A complete tree can be addressed arithmetically, saving all the pointer storage.
hint: What does having no gaps let you do with indices?

body: What problem does a segment tree solve that a prefix-sum array cannot?

options.body: Range queries on data that also changes

options.whyWrong: Prefix sums handle exactly that case, more cheaply.

options.body: Finding the maximum of the whole array
options.whyWrong: A single scan does that; neither structure is needed.
Neither structure sorts anything.

explanation: A prefix-sum array must be rebuilt in O(n) after any update. A segment tree answers a range query and applies a point update both in O(log n), which is what makes it the right choice when reads and writes are interleaved.
concept: Choose the structure by the read/write mix, not by the query alone.
hint: What happens to a prefix array when one element changes?

body: Which traversal finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph?

options.whyWrong: DFS reaches every node but the first path it finds is not necessarily the shortest.

options.body: Either, since both visit every node
options.whyWrong: Visiting every node is not the same as finding shortest paths.

explanation: BFS explores by increasing distance from the source, so the first time it reaches a node it has done so in the fewest possible edges. With weights this no longer holds and you need Dijkstra.
concept: BFS layers the graph by hop count, which is exactly shortest path when every edge costs the same.
hint: In what order does BFS reach nodes?

body: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph using DFS?

options.body: Look for an edge back to a node currently on the recursion stack

options.whyWrong: A visited node may be finished and on a different branch — that is a cross edge, not a cycle.

options.body: Count edges and compare with nodes
options.whyWrong: The edge count relates to cycles in undirected graphs, not directed ones.

options.whyWrong: A node with in-degree zero says nothing about cycles elsewhere.

explanation: A cycle exists exactly when DFS finds a back edge — an edge to a node that is grey, meaning it is an ancestor still being explored. Tracking three colours (unvisited, in progress, done) distinguishes that from an edge to a finished node.

hint: What is the difference between a node you have finished and one you are still inside?

body: Dijkstra’s algorithm gives wrong answers on graphs with what property?

options.whyWrong: Dijkstra handles cycles fine as long as weights are non-negative.
Ties are not a problem; any one of them is returned.
Unreachable nodes simply keep an infinite distance.

explanation: Dijkstra finalises a node’s distance the moment it is popped, assuming no later path can improve it. A negative edge can do exactly that, so the assumption breaks. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and detects negative cycles.
concept: Dijkstra’s greedy choice depends on edge weights never being negative.
hint: What lets Dijkstra treat a popped node as settled?

body: A topological sort exists for a directed graph if and only if it is what?

options.whyWrong: A DAG with several components still has a valid topological order.
Weights play no part in topological ordering.
A complete directed graph contains cycles and has no topological order.

explanation: A cycle would require each of its nodes to come before the others, which is impossible in a linear order. On a DAG, Kahn’s algorithm or a DFS finishing order produces a valid sequence — which is how build systems and course prerequisites are resolved.
concept: Topological order is exactly a linearisation of a partial order, which cycles destroy.
hint: Could a node in a cycle ever come first?

body: What is the space complexity of BFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges?

options.whyWrong: The queue holds vertices, not edges; the adjacency structure is separate from the traversal’s own space.
A queue and a visited set both grow with the graph.
