explanation: BFS stores a visited marker per vertex and a queue that in the worst case holds a whole level, which is O(V). DFS is also O(V) for the recursion stack, though the constant differs — on a wide shallow graph BFS uses more, on a deep narrow one DFS uses more.
concept: Traversal space is dominated by the frontier plus the visited set.
hint: What is in the queue at any moment?

body: Union-Find with path compression and union by rank gives what amortised time per operation?

options.whyWrong: That is what union by rank alone gives; path compression improves it further.
Linear per operation is the naive version with no optimisation at all.
That is a total sorting cost, not a per-operation bound.

explanation: The combination yields O(α(n)) amortised, where α is the inverse Ackermann function — below 5 for any input that fits in the universe. This is why Kruskal’s algorithm is dominated by its sorting step rather than by the union-find work.
concept: Union-Find is the standard structure for dynamic connectivity and Kruskal’s MST.
hint: How fast does the inverse Ackermann function grow?

body: What two properties must a problem have for dynamic programming to apply?

options.whyWrong: Neither is required; DP applies to unsorted data with repeats.

options.body: A greedy choice and a base case
options.whyWrong: A greedy choice property means you can skip DP entirely.
Neither is a condition for DP.

explanation: Optimal substructure means an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to subproblems; overlapping subproblems means the same subproblem recurs, which is what memoisation exploits. Divide and conquer has the first without the second, which is why merge sort is not DP.
concept: DP = recursion + reuse. Without overlap, memoising buys nothing.
hint: What distinguishes DP from plain divide and conquer?

body: What is the difference between top-down and bottom-up dynamic programming?

options.body: Top-down memoises a recursion; bottom-up fills a table iteratively

options.whyWrong: Bottom-up usually has lower constant factors because it avoids call overhead.

options.body: Bottom-up uses less memory by definition
options.whyWrong: Both store the same table unless you additionally apply rolling-array optimisation.

options.whyWrong: They are two implementations of the same recurrence.

explanation: Top-down starts from the original problem and recurses, caching results as it goes, so it only computes the states it actually needs. Bottom-up computes every state in dependency order, avoids recursion depth limits, and is easier to optimise for space.
concept: Same recurrence, two evaluation orders, different practical trade-offs.
hint: Which one might skip states it never needs?

body: The 0/1 knapsack DP runs in O(n × W). Why is this called pseudo-polynomial rather than polynomial?

options.body: W is a value, and its size in bits is log W — so the cost is exponential in the input length
Because it uses a two-dimensional table
options.whyWrong: Table dimensionality does not determine the complexity class.

options.body: Because it is only an approximation
options.whyWrong: The DP is exact, not approximate.

options.body: Because it fails for large n

explanation: Complexity is measured against the input encoding length. A capacity of one billion is only about 30 bits, yet the table has a billion columns — so the running time is exponential in the number of bits. This is why 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard despite the DP.
concept: Pseudo-polynomial means polynomial in the numeric value, exponential in its encoded size.
hint: How many bits does it take to write down W?

body: In the longest common subsequence DP, what does dp[i][j] represent?

options.body: The LCS length of the first i characters of one string and the first j of the other
Whether characters i and j are equal
options.whyWrong: That is a single comparison used to compute the cell, not what it stores.

options.body: The edit distance between the two prefixes
options.whyWrong: Edit distance is a related but different recurrence.

options.body: The number of distinct common subsequences
options.whyWrong: Counting subsequences is a different problem with a different recurrence.

concept: Getting the state definition right is most of the work in a DP problem.
hint: What are the two things a subproblem here depends on?

body: Many 2-D DP tables can be reduced to O(n) space. What makes that possible?

options.body: Each row depends only on the previous row

options.whyWrong: Symmetry is not general, and even when present does not reduce the asymptotic space.
Value magnitude affects word size, not the number of cells.

options.body: The answer is always in the last cell
options.whyWrong: Where the answer sits does not let you discard earlier rows.

explanation: If the recurrence only reaches back one row, you can keep two rows — or even one, updating in the right direction. Space drops from O(n × m) to O(m). The catch is that you lose the ability to reconstruct the actual solution path, only its value.
concept: Rolling arrays trade the reconstruction trace for memory.
hint: How far back does the recurrence actually look?

body: Which problem does NOT have optimal substructure?

options.body: Longest simple path in a general graph

options.whyWrong: Sub-paths of shortest paths are themselves shortest paths.
Its optimal parenthesisation is built from optimal sub-parenthesisations.
Its recurrence is a textbook example of optimal substructure.

explanation: Combining two optimal longest simple paths can revisit a vertex, making the result not simple — so the optimum of the whole is not built from optima of the parts. This is why longest path is NP-hard while shortest path is easy.

hint: What goes wrong when you join two long paths together?

body: Memoisation converts the naive recursive Fibonacci from exponential to what?

options.whyWrong: Logarithmic time needs the matrix-power or fast-doubling method, not simple memoisation.
Each of the n states is computed once in constant time, so the total is linear.
Caching is precisely what removes the repeated subtrees.

explanation: There are only n distinct subproblems, each computed once and thereafter returned from the cache, so the work is proportional to the number of states. The same counting argument — states × cost per state — gives the complexity of most DP solutions.
concept: DP cost = number of distinct states × work per state.
hint: How many different values can fib() be called with?

body: What does O(n) formally describe?

options.body: An upper bound on growth, up to a constant factor, for large n

options.whyWrong: Big-O discards constants and lower-order terms, so it is not an exact count.
Best case is described separately; O() can be applied to any case you choose to analyse.
O() notation describes any resource; which one depends on what you are bounding.

explanation: f(n) is O(g(n)) if beyond some n₀ it stays below c·g(n) for a constant c. That is why O(n) is technically also a valid (loose) bound on an O(log n) algorithm — Θ is the notation for a tight bound.
concept: Big-O is an upper bound; Θ is tight; Ω is a lower bound.
hint: Is O() a ceiling, a floor, or an exact figure?

body: What is the time complexity of a loop that halves n each iteration until it reaches 1?

options.whyWrong: Linear cost would mean one iteration per element, but halving skips most of them.
That would need a linear amount of work inside each of the log n iterations.
The iteration count grows with n, slowly but without bound.

explanation: Halving repeatedly from n reaches 1 after about log₂ n steps. The base of the logarithm only changes the constant factor, which is why it is conventionally omitted.

hint: How many times can you halve 1024?

body: Two nested loops, the inner running to i where the outer runs to n. What is the complexity?

options.whyWrong: The inner loop runs a different number of times on each pass, so the total exceeds n.
No halving or sorting step is present.
Only two loops are involved.

explanation: The inner loop runs 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2 times, which is n²/2 — still O(n²) once the constant is dropped. A triangular loop is asymptotically the same as a square one.
concept: Constant factors are discarded, so half a square is still quadratic.
hint: Add up the iteration counts rather than multiplying the bounds.

body: What is the complexity of appending n items to a list one at a time, where each append is amortised O(1)?

options.whyWrong: That would be the cost if every append copied the whole list, which amortisation avoids.
Fewer than n operations cannot complete n appends.
Nothing here sorts or halves.

explanation: Amortised O(1) per operation means n operations total O(n), even though individual appends occasionally trigger an O(n) resize. Amortised analysis is about the total across a sequence, not a guarantee for each call.
concept: Amortised cost is meaningful for a sequence of operations, not a single one.
hint: What does "amortised" let you multiply out?

body: An algorithm runs in O(2^n). Roughly what is the largest n that finishes in a second at a billion operations per second?

options.whyWrong: 2^1000 exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe.
2^100 is around 10^30 operations — far beyond a second.

hint: What power of two is about a billion?

body: Which is asymptotically fastest for large n: O(n log n), O(n^1.5), or O(n²)?

options.whyWrong: They separate clearly as n grows; the differences are not constant factors.

body: What does it mean when an algorithm is described as O(1) space?

options.whyWrong: Every algorithm uses some memory; the point is that the amount is bounded.

options.whyWrong: The input itself is not counted as extra space in this convention.

hint: Does the count of extra variables depend on n?

body: What is a hash collision?

options.body: Two different keys producing the same hash value

options.whyWrong: Hash functions map inputs of any size to a fixed range.

body: What is the load factor of a hash table?

options.whyWrong: That is the reciprocal, which is not the standard definition.

hint: What ratio tells you how crowded the table is?

body: Which is a requirement of a good hash function for a hash table?

body: Why must an object’s hashCode be consistent with its equals method?

hint: How does a lookup narrow the search before comparing?

body: Open addressing resolves collisions how?

hint: Where does the colliding entry actually go?

body: When is a hash map the wrong choice compared with a balanced tree map?

body: What is the average time to find the first non-repeating character in a string using a hash map?

explanation: Advancing one pointer by one node and another by two means the fast pointer gains one position per step inside any cycle, so it must eventually meet the slow one. If it reaches the end instead, there is no cycle.
concept: Two pointers at different speeds is the standard O(1)-space cycle test.
hint: What happens to the gap between them once both are inside a loop?

body: Reversing a singly linked list iteratively requires how many pointers?

options.whyWrong: With one pointer you lose the rest of the list the moment you rewrite a link.
Two is nearly enough, but you still need to save the next node before overwriting the current link.
Storing every node would be O(n) space; the point of the iterative version is O(1).

explanation: At each step you save next = current.next, point current.next at previous, then advance previous and current. Losing the next pointer before reassigning is the classic bug.
concept: Rewriting a link requires saving what it pointed at first.
hint: What do you lose the instant you overwrite current.next?

body: Which problem is a stack the natural fit for?

options.body: Checking whether brackets in an expression are balanced

options.whyWrong: That is first-in-first-out, which is a queue.
That calls for a heap.

options.body: Looking up a value by key
options.whyWrong: That calls for a hash map.

explanation: Each closing bracket must match the most recently opened unclosed one, which is exactly last-in-first-out. Push on open, pop and compare on close, and require the stack to be empty at the end.
concept: Whenever "most recent unmatched thing" appears in a problem, think stack.
hint: Which bracket does a closing one have to match?

body: A queue implemented with two stacks has what amortised cost per operation?

options.whyWrong: Only occasional dequeues trigger a transfer, and each element moves at most twice overall.
No halving occurs anywhere in the construction.
Enqueue is a single push onto the inbox stack.

explanation: Push onto an inbox stack; to dequeue, pour the inbox into an outbox only when the outbox is empty, then pop. Each element is pushed and popped at most twice in total, so n operations cost O(n) — constant amortised.
concept: Amortised analysis again: an occasional expensive transfer averaged over many cheap operations.
hint: How many times can a single element move between the stacks?

body: What does a min-heap guarantee?

options.body: Every parent is less than or equal to its children
The array is fully sorted ascending
options.whyWrong: A heap is only partially ordered; heapsort is what turns it into a sorted array.

options.body: The smallest element is at the end
options.whyWrong: The minimum sits at the root, which is index 0.
A heap is a complete tree, so the last level may be partly filled.

explanation: The heap property constrains parent and child only, which is why the minimum is at the root and can be read in O(1). No ordering is implied between siblings, and that weaker invariant is exactly what makes insert and extract O(log n).
concept: A heap is partially ordered — strong enough to find the extreme, weak enough to maintain cheaply.
hint: Does the heap property say anything about two siblings?

body: To find the k largest elements of n items efficiently, which structure do you use and of what size?

options.whyWrong: A max-heap of size k makes the largest easy to see but the wrong element cheap to evict.
Building a heap of everything is O(n) space and unnecessary when k is small.

options.body: A sorted array of size n
options.whyWrong: Sorting everything is O(n log n) versus O(n log k).

explanation: Keep a min-heap of the k best so far. Its root is the weakest of them, so a new element is compared with the root and replaces it if larger. Cost is O(n log k) with O(k) space — a clear win when k is much smaller than n.
concept: For "top k", hold a heap whose root is the item you would evict next.
hint: Which of your k candidates do you need instant access to?

body: What is a race condition?

options.body: Two threads access shared data concurrently and the result depends on their timing
A thread that runs faster than expected
options.whyWrong: Speed alone is not a defect; the bug is the unsynchronised shared access.
Deadlock is threads blocked forever; a race produces wrong results while still running.

options.body: A process using more CPU than its share
options.whyWrong: That is a scheduling fairness issue, not a correctness one.

explanation: The classic example is two threads doing counter++ — a read, an increment and a write that can interleave so one update is lost. Fixing it needs mutual exclusion or an atomic operation, not merely making the code faster.
concept: A race is a correctness bug caused by unsynchronised shared mutable state.
hint: Why is counter++ not a single indivisible step?

body: What is the difference between a mutex and a semaphore?

options.body: A mutex has an owner and allows one holder; a counting semaphore permits N

options.whyWrong: Relative speed depends on the implementation and is not the conceptual difference.

options.body: A mutex works only between processes
options.whyWrong: Mutexes are typically within a process; semaphores are often the cross-process tool.

options.body: They are the same thing with different names
options.whyWrong: Ownership and counting are real behavioural differences — only the owner may unlock a mutex.

explanation: A mutex enforces mutual exclusion and is released by the thread that took it, which allows priority inheritance. A semaphore is a counter that any thread may signal, so it also models a pool of N resources or a producer-consumer handoff.
concept: Mutex = ownership and exclusion. Semaphore = counting and signalling.
hint: Can one thread release a lock another thread took?

body: Which four conditions must all hold for deadlock to occur?

options.body: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait

options.whyWrong: These are all real problems, but none is a Coffman condition.
These describe concurrency issues generally, not the deadlock conditions.
These are ordinary OS mechanisms unrelated to deadlock.

explanation: These are the Coffman conditions, and they are necessary together — breaking any one prevents deadlock. Requiring all locks to be taken in a global order is the usual practical fix, since it eliminates circular wait.
concept: Deadlock prevention works by making one of the four conditions impossible.
hint: Which one is easiest to eliminate by convention in application code?

body: What is thrashing?

options.body: The system spends more time paging than executing
Two threads repeatedly locking and unlocking
options.whyWrong: That is lock contention, a different problem.

options.body: The CPU switching between processes too often
options.whyWrong: Excessive context switching is related but distinct; thrashing is specifically about paging.
A hardware fault is not thrashing.

explanation: When the combined working set exceeds physical memory, each process evicts pages another needs immediately, so page faults cascade and CPU utilisation collapses. The fix is to reduce the degree of multiprogramming or add memory — not to schedule harder.
concept: Thrashing is a symptom of the working set exceeding available frames.
hint: What is the machine actually busy doing?

body: What does a page table map?

options.body: Virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers

options.whyWrong: That mapping is kept by the swap subsystem, not the page table.
That is a directory, part of the filesystem.
Limits live in the process control block.

explanation: Each process has its own page table, which is what gives it a private address space. Because a lookup would otherwise cost an extra memory access, the TLB caches recent translations.
concept: Virtual memory is an indirection layer that buys isolation and the illusion of contiguity.
hint: What makes two processes able to use the same address safely?

body: Which scheduling algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time?

options.whyWrong: FCFS suffers the convoy effect — one long job delays everything behind it.
Round Robin optimises responsiveness and fairness, not average waiting time.
Priority optimises for importance and can starve low-priority jobs entirely.

explanation: SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time, but it requires knowing each job’s length in advance, which is why real schedulers estimate it from recent behaviour instead. It can also starve long jobs indefinitely.
concept: Optimal on paper, unimplementable as stated — the reason real schedulers approximate it.
hint: What information does it need that a real OS does not have?

body: What is the main difference between a process and a thread?

options.body: Threads within a process share an address space; processes do not

options.whyWrong: Threads run in parallel on multiple cores; that is much of the point.
Process creation and context switching are heavier, not faster.
Threads are the unit of scheduling on most modern systems.

explanation: Shared memory makes thread communication cheap and thread bugs dangerous — one thread can corrupt another’s data. Processes are isolated, so a crash is contained, at the cost of slower creation and explicit IPC.
concept: Sharing is the whole trade-off: cheap communication versus contained failure.
hint: What can one thread accidentally overwrite that one process cannot?

body: What is a context switch?

options.body: Saving one execution context and restoring another so a different task can run
Moving a process from disk to memory
options.whyWrong: That is swapping, a memory-management operation.

options.body: Switching a process from user mode to kernel mode
options.whyWrong: That is a mode switch, which is cheaper and does not change which process runs.
Repriorisation may cause a context switch but is not one.

explanation: The kernel saves registers, the program counter and memory-management state, then loads another task’s. It is pure overhead — and it also invalidates cache and TLB entries, which is often the larger hidden cost.
concept: Context switches are overhead; reducing them is why thread pools and async I/O exist.
hint: Is any useful work being done during it?

body: A process is in the "ready" state. What does that mean?

options.body: It could run immediately but no CPU is currently free for it
It is waiting for I/O to finish
options.whyWrong: That is the blocked or waiting state.
That is the terminated state.

options.body: It has not been created yet
options.whyWrong: That is the new state.

explanation: Ready means runnable but not running — everything it needs is available except a CPU. Blocked is different: even given a CPU it could not proceed, because it is waiting for something external.
concept: The distinction between ready and blocked is what the scheduler’s queues are built on.
hint: If a CPU freed up this instant, could it run?

body: What problem does normalisation to third normal form address?

options.body: Update anomalies caused by redundantly stored data

options.whyWrong: Normalisation often makes reads slower by requiring joins; denormalisation is the performance move.
Space is a minor side benefit, not the purpose.
Those are handled by locking and isolation levels.

explanation: If a department’s address is repeated on every employee row, changing it means updating many rows and risking inconsistency. 3NF removes transitive dependencies on the key so each fact is stored once — the trade-off being more joins at read time.
concept: Normalisation optimises for write correctness; denormalisation optimises for read speed.
hint: What goes wrong when the same fact is stored in fifty places?

body: What does the "I" in ACID guarantee?

options.body: Concurrent transactions do not see each other’s partial results
Every transaction is written to disk immediately
options.whyWrong: That is durability, the D.

options.body: The database never violates a constraint
options.whyWrong: That is consistency, the C.

options.body: A transaction either fully completes or has no effect
options.whyWrong: That is atomicity, the A.

explanation: Isolation means concurrent transactions produce a result equivalent to some serial order. In practice databases offer weaker levels — read committed, repeatable read — trading isolation for throughput, which is why phantom reads and lost updates remain real concerns.
concept: Isolation is a spectrum in practice, not the binary the acronym suggests.
hint: Which letter is about what other transactions can see?

body: Why does adding an index speed up reads but slow down writes?

options.body: The index is a second structure that must be kept in step on every modification
Indexes lock the table during reads
options.whyWrong: A read does not lock the table in normal operation.

options.body: Indexes are stored on slower disk
options.whyWrong: They live on the same storage as the table.

options.body: Indexes have to be rebuilt on every query
options.whyWrong: They are maintained on write, not rebuilt on read.

explanation: A B-tree index turns a full scan into a logarithmic descent, but every insert, update or delete must also update that tree — and every additional index multiplies that cost. Which is why indexing every column is a common and expensive mistake.
concept: Each index is a read optimisation paid for on every write.
hint: What has to happen to the index when a row changes?

body: In an ER diagram, what does a many-to-many relationship require in the physical schema?

options.body: A junction table holding a foreign key to each side
A foreign key on the more important table
options.whyWrong: A single foreign key column can only reference one row, so it cannot express many-to-many.

options.body: A composite primary key on one table
options.whyWrong: A composite key does not by itself relate two tables.

options.body: Nothing — relational databases support it directly
options.whyWrong: Relational tables have no native many-to-many construct.

explanation: Enrolments between students and courses need their own table with student_id and course_id, usually with that pair as the primary key. The junction table is also the natural place for attributes of the relationship itself, such as an enrolment date.
concept: Many-to-many always becomes a third table in a relational schema.
hint: Where would you record the date a student joined a course?

body: What is a deadlock in a database, and how do most engines handle it?

options.body: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs; the engine detects it and aborts one
Two queries reading the same row; the engine queues them
options.whyWrong: Concurrent reads do not conflict under normal isolation levels.

options.body: A query running too long; the engine kills it
options.whyWrong: That is a statement timeout, not a deadlock.

options.body: A table growing beyond its file limit; the engine extends it
options.whyWrong: That is a storage matter, unrelated to locking.

explanation: The engine maintains a wait-for graph and looks for a cycle. On finding one it picks a victim — usually the transaction with the least work done — and rolls it back with a deadlock error, expecting the application to retry. Consistent lock ordering is what avoids the situation.
concept: Application code that touches rows in a consistent order is the real fix; retry is the safety net.
hint: What does the engine do once it finds a cycle?

body: What is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN?

options.body: LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched rows from the left table, filling the right side with NULLs

options.whyWrong: Performance depends on indexes and data, not on the join type alone.

options.body: INNER JOIN can only join two tables
options.whyWrong: Both can chain across many tables.
Neither join deduplicates; that is what DISTINCT or GROUP BY do.

explanation: INNER JOIN returns only rows matching on both sides. LEFT JOIN returns every left row regardless, which is how you find customers with no orders — LEFT JOIN then filter on the right side being NULL.
concept: A LEFT JOIN plus an IS NULL filter is the standard "find rows with no match" idiom.
hint: How would you list customers who have never ordered?

body: Why does filtering a LEFT JOIN’s right table in WHERE often turn it into an INNER JOIN?

options.body: The unmatched rows have NULL there, and a NULL comparison in WHERE is not true
Because WHERE runs before the join
options.whyWrong: The join happens first; WHERE filters the result.

options.body: Because LEFT JOIN is only a hint
options.whyWrong: It is not a hint; the engine honours it.

options.body: Because NULLs are converted to zero
options.whyWrong: SQL does not silently convert NULL to zero.

explanation: A left row with no match gets NULL in every right-hand column, and `WHERE r.status = 'active'` is unknown for NULL, so the row is dropped — exactly what INNER JOIN would have done. Putting the condition in the ON clause instead preserves the unmatched rows.
concept: Conditions on the right table belong in ON; conditions on the left belong in WHERE.
hint: What does status = 'active' evaluate to when status is NULL?

body: What does GROUP BY do, and what may the SELECT list then contain?

options.body: Collapses rows into groups; SELECT may list grouping columns and aggregates
Sorts the result; SELECT may contain anything
options.whyWrong: GROUP BY is not a sort, and the SELECT list is constrained.

options.body: Removes duplicates; SELECT may contain anything
options.whyWrong: Deduplication is DISTINCT, and the constraint still applies.

options.body: Joins tables; SELECT may contain any joined column
options.whyWrong: GROUP BY does not join anything.

explanation: Each group becomes one output row, so a non-grouped, non-aggregated column has no single well-defined value. Strict engines reject it; MySQL historically returned an arbitrary row’s value, which is a common source of silently wrong reports.
concept: If a column is neither grouped nor aggregated, the query has not said which value it means.
hint: If a group has five rows, which one’s name would you print?

body: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

options.body: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation

options.whyWrong: They apply at different stages, so swapping them changes results or raises an error.

options.body: HAVING works only with ORDER BY
options.whyWrong: HAVING is tied to GROUP BY, not ORDER BY.

options.body: WHERE cannot be used with joins
options.whyWrong: WHERE is used with joins constantly.

explanation: You cannot filter on COUNT(*) in WHERE because the count does not exist yet. Filtering early in WHERE is also usually faster, since fewer rows reach the grouping step.
concept: Know the logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY.
hint: Where would you put "only groups with more than five rows"?

body: What does a window function do that GROUP BY cannot?

options.body: Compute an aggregate while keeping every individual row

options.whyWrong: Both operate on the result set; neither is limited to one table.
Window functions are not inherently faster.
Window functions compute values; filtering still needs WHERE or a wrapping query.

explanation: SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) puts the department total on every employee row, so you can show a salary next to its department average without a self-join. GROUP BY would collapse those rows away.
concept: Window functions add context to rows instead of replacing them.
hint: How would you show each row next to its group’s average?

body: What is a correlated subquery?

options.body: A subquery that references a column from the outer query, so it runs per outer row
A subquery that returns more than one row
options.whyWrong: Row count does not determine correlation.

options.body: A subquery in the FROM clause
options.whyWrong: That is a derived table, which is not correlated.
Self-joins are a different construct.

explanation: Because it depends on the current outer row, it is conceptually evaluated once per row, which can be slow. Query planners often rewrite these as joins or semi-joins — and rewriting one by hand as a JOIN is a common optimisation.
concept: Correlated subqueries are readable but can hide a per-row cost.
hint: What makes the subquery unable to be evaluated just once?

body: Which query finds the second-highest salary safely when duplicates exist?

options.body: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp)
SELECT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
options.whyWrong: With duplicate top salaries this returns the same value again rather than the second distinct one.

options.body: SELECT TOP 2 salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC
options.whyWrong: This returns two rows, and the same duplicate problem applies.

options.body: SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE ROWNUM = 2
options.whyWrong: ROWNUM is assigned before ordering, so this is unreliable.

explanation: Taking the maximum below the overall maximum skips ties correctly and returns NULL rather than an error when there is no second salary. DENSE_RANK() = 2 is the modern equivalent and generalises to the Nth case.
concept: Ranking questions turn on how ties should be treated — decide that before writing the query.
hint: What happens to LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 when two people share the top salary?

body: In C, what does `int *p; *p = 5;` do?

options.body: Undefined behaviour — p was never pointed at valid memory

options.whyWrong: That would be p = 5, not *p = 5.
Declaring a pointer allocates no target; malloc or an address is needed.
An uninitialised pointer is not inert — dereferencing it writes to whatever address it happens to hold.

explanation: p holds an indeterminate address, so writing through it may crash, corrupt unrelated memory, or appear to work — the last being the most dangerous. Pointers must be given a valid target before dereferencing.
concept: Declaring a pointer reserves space for an address, not for what it points at.
hint: What address does p hold before you assign one?

body: What is printed by: `int i = 5; printf("%d %d", i++, ++i);` in C?

options.body: Undefined — i is modified twice without an intervening sequence point

options.whyWrong: This is one plausible output, but the standard does not guarantee it.
Also plausible on some compilers, and equally not guaranteed.
Another possible observed result, still undefined behaviour.

explanation: Argument evaluation order is unspecified and modifying i twice between sequence points is undefined behaviour. Different compilers and optimisation levels legitimately print different things. Interviewers ask this to see whether you recognise UB rather than memorise one compiler’s answer.
concept: "What does my compiler print" and "what does the standard guarantee" are different questions.
hint: How many times is i modified in one expression?

body: In Java, what does `String s = "a"; s.concat("b"); System.out.println(s);` print?

options.whyWrong: concat returns a new string; it cannot modify s because Strings are immutable.
No space is introduced anywhere.
The code compiles fine — it just discards the result.

explanation: Strings are immutable, so concat returns a new object and leaves s untouched. The returned value is discarded. Writing s = s.concat("b") is what the author intended.
concept: Methods on immutable types return new values rather than mutating in place.
hint: What happens to the value concat returns?

body: What is the difference between pass by value and pass by reference for an object in Java?

options.body: Java always passes the reference by value — you can mutate the object but not rebind the caller’s variable

options.whyWrong: If it did, reassigning the parameter would change the caller’s variable, which it does not.

options.body: Java passes a deep copy of the object
options.whyWrong: No copy of the object is made; only the reference is copied.

options.body: It depends on whether the object is final
options.whyWrong: final affects rebinding of the variable, not the calling convention.

explanation: The method gets its own copy of the reference. Calling list.add(x) affects the caller’s list because both references point at the same object; writing list = new ArrayList<>() inside the method affects nothing outside it.
concept: "Pass reference by value" explains both behaviours that seem contradictory.
hint: What happens if the method assigns a whole new object to the parameter?

body: What is a memory leak in a garbage-collected language?

options.body: Objects stay reachable from a live reference long after they are needed

options.whyWrong: There is no free to call; the collector reclaims unreachable memory automatically.
A collector fault is a different failure entirely.
Stack and native allocations are not what leak in this sense.

explanation: A collector frees what is unreachable, so anything still referenced stays alive. A static list that only ever grows, an unremoved listener, or a cache with no eviction policy are the classic culprits — the memory is not lost, it is retained.
concept: In managed languages, leaks are unintended retention rather than unfreed allocations.
hint: What decides whether the collector can reclaim an object?

body: What does `static` mean for a class member in Java or C++?

options.body: It belongs to the class itself rather than to any instance

options.whyWrong: That is const or final; static members are freely mutable.

options.body: It is private to the file
options.whyWrong: That is C’s file-scope static, a different meaning of the keyword.

options.body: It is allocated on the stack
options.whyWrong: Static members live for the program’s duration, not in a stack frame.

explanation: One copy exists regardless of how many instances are created, and it can be accessed without an instance. That single shared copy is also why mutable static state is a common source of thread-safety bugs.
concept: Static means "one per class", which is exactly why it needs care under concurrency.
hint: How many copies exist if you create a thousand objects?

body: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle require?

options.body: A subclass must be usable anywhere its parent is, without breaking behaviour
A subclass must override every parent method
options.whyWrong: Overriding everything is neither required nor desirable.

options.body: A class must have only one reason to change
options.whyWrong: That is the Single Responsibility Principle.

options.body: Classes should depend on interfaces rather than concrete types
options.whyWrong: That is the Dependency Inversion Principle.

explanation: The classic violation is Square extending Rectangle: code that sets width and height independently and expects both to hold breaks when handed a Square. Inheritance must preserve the contract, not merely reuse the fields.
concept: Inheritance is a promise about behaviour, not a shortcut for sharing code.
hint: Can every Rectangle be replaced by a Square without surprising the caller?

body: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?

options.body: An abstract class can hold state and constructors; an interface primarily declares a contract
Interfaces cannot have any method bodies
options.whyWrong: Modern Java and C# allow default implementations in interfaces.

options.body: Abstract classes cannot have concrete methods
options.whyWrong: They very often do — that is a common reason to use one.
Single versus multiple inheritance alone makes them different design choices.

explanation: A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one abstract class, so interfaces express capabilities while abstract classes express a partial implementation with shared state. Preferring interfaces keeps the hierarchy flexible.
concept: Interface = what it can do. Abstract class = shared partial implementation.
hint: How many of each can one class inherit from?

body: What is composition over inheritance?

options.body: Building behaviour by holding other objects rather than extending a base class
Avoiding classes entirely in favour of functions
options.whyWrong: That is a different paradigm shift, not what this principle says.
Sealing classes is a related tactic but not the principle itself.

options.body: Using multiple inheritance instead of single
options.whyWrong: Multiple inheritance is still inheritance and compounds its problems.

explanation: Inheritance binds a subclass to its parent’s implementation, so a parent change can break it — the fragile base class problem. Composition delegates to a held object, which can be swapped at runtime and tested independently.
concept: Prefer "has a" to "is a" unless the subtype genuinely satisfies the parent’s contract.
hint: What happens to every subclass when the base class changes?

body: Method overloading is resolved when?

options.body: At compile time, from the declared argument types
At runtime, from the actual object types
options.whyWrong: That is overriding, which is dynamic dispatch.
Linking does not perform method selection.

options.body: Only when the method is first called
options.whyWrong: JIT compilation does not change which overload was selected.

explanation: Overloading is static polymorphism: the compiler picks the overload from the static types of the arguments. Overriding is dynamic: the runtime type decides. This is why passing a variable declared as Object to an overloaded method picks the Object overload even if it holds a String.
concept: Overload = compile time on declared types. Override = runtime on actual type.
hint: Does the compiler know the runtime type of a variable?

body: What problem does a cache primarily solve, and what does it cost you?

options.body: It cuts latency and load, at the cost of possible staleness
It increases storage capacity, at the cost of speed
options.whyWrong: A cache trades space for speed, not the other way round.

options.body: It guarantees consistency, at the cost of memory
options.whyWrong: Caching weakens consistency rather than guaranteeing it.

options.body: It removes the need for a database
options.whyWrong: A cache is a front for a source of truth, never a replacement.

explanation: Serving from memory avoids a slower call, but the cached copy can diverge from the source. Every caching design is really a decision about how stale is acceptable and how invalidation happens — which is why cache invalidation is proverbially hard.
concept: A cache is a deliberate trade of consistency for latency.
hint: What can go wrong when the underlying data changes?

body: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?

options.body: Horizontal adds more machines; vertical makes one machine bigger
Horizontal adds more disks; vertical adds more RAM
options.whyWrong: Both are ways of making a single machine bigger — both are vertical.

options.body: Horizontal is for databases; vertical is for web servers
options.whyWrong: Either approach applies to either tier.
It is often cheaper at scale but adds coordination complexity that vertical scaling avoids.

explanation: Vertical scaling is simpler but has a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling is effectively unbounded but forces you to handle statelessness, load balancing and data partitioning.
concept: Vertical is simpler; horizontal is unbounded. The complexity is the price.
hint: Which one eventually runs out of headroom?

body: Why is a REST API usually designed to be stateless?

options.body: Any server can handle any request, which makes horizontal scaling straightforward

options.whyWrong: Stateless requests are typically larger, since they carry their own context.

options.body: It removes the need for authentication
options.whyWrong: Every request still authenticates — it just carries the credential each time.
Idempotency is a property of the method, not of statelessness.

explanation: With no server-side session, a load balancer can route a request anywhere and a server can restart without losing anyone’s progress. The cost is that each request must carry its context, typically a token.
concept: Statelessness is what makes servers interchangeable.
hint: What breaks if the load balancer sends the next request elsewhere?

body: What does database sharding do?

options.body: Splits rows across several databases by a shard key
Copies the whole database to several servers
options.whyWrong: That is replication, which addresses read load and availability rather than size.
Compression is unrelated to sharding.

options.body: Splits the columns of a table
options.whyWrong: Splitting columns is vertical partitioning, a different technique.

explanation: Each shard holds a disjoint subset, so writes and storage scale beyond one machine. The costs are real: cross-shard queries and transactions become hard, and a poorly chosen shard key creates hotspots that are painful to fix later.
concept: Sharding scales writes; replication scales reads. They solve different problems.
hint: What happens to a query that needs rows from every shard?

body: Which HTTP method should be idempotent?

options.whyWrong: POST is the conventional non-idempotent method — repeating it usually creates another resource.
PATCH is not required to be idempotent, though a given implementation may be.
CONNECT establishes a tunnel and is not part of the resource semantics being asked about.

explanation: PUT replaces a resource with the supplied representation, so sending it twice leaves the same state as sending it once. That matters because a client that times out cannot tell whether the request arrived, and idempotency makes retrying safe.
concept: Idempotency is what makes a retry policy safe to implement.
hint: What should a client do when it does not know whether its request landed?

body: What is the purpose of the TLB?

options.body: To cache recent virtual-to-physical address translations
To cache recently used file blocks
options.whyWrong: That is the page cache or buffer cache.

options.body: To store the process control block
options.whyWrong: The PCB lives in kernel memory, not in a translation cache.

options.body: To hold instructions waiting to execute
options.whyWrong: That is the instruction pipeline or prefetch buffer.

explanation: Without it, every memory access would need an extra access to read the page table. The TLB is a small associative cache of translations, and a miss costs a page-table walk — which is why TLB flushes on context switch are expensive.
concept: Virtual memory needs a translation cache or the indirection would double every memory access.
hint: What extra work does address translation add to each access?

body: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?

options.body: Preemptive can interrupt a running process; non-preemptive waits for it to yield
Preemptive is only used on multi-core systems
options.whyWrong: Preemption predates multi-core and is used on single cores too.
It avoids switching overhead but responds far worse to interactive work.
Memory use is not the distinction.

explanation: Preemption lets the OS enforce fairness and responsiveness by taking the CPU back on a timer. Non-preemptive scheduling has lower overhead but one misbehaving process can hold the CPU indefinitely.
concept: Preemption buys responsiveness at the cost of context-switch overhead.
hint: What happens if a process never yields?

body: What is a semaphore’s "wait" (P) operation?

options.body: Decrement the counter, blocking while it would go negative

options.whyWrong: That is the signal or V operation.
No semaphore operation zeroes the counter.
Reading the value without changing it is not P.

explanation: P decrements and blocks if no permit is available; V increments and wakes a waiter. Both must be atomic — a non-atomic check-then-decrement reintroduces exactly the race the semaphore exists to prevent.
concept: The atomicity of P and V is what makes the primitive work at all.
hint: What breaks if the check and the decrement are separate steps?

body: Why can a spinlock be better than a mutex in kernel code?

options.body: When the wait is very short, spinning avoids the cost of sleeping and waking

options.whyWrong: They deadlock just as readily, and worse, they burn CPU while doing it.
Both can be shared across processes given shared memory.
A spinlock is built from an atomic test-and-set.

explanation: Blocking a thread costs two context switches. If the critical section is a handful of instructions, spinning is cheaper. It is a poor choice when the hold time is long or on a single core, where the spinner prevents the holder from running.
concept: Spin when the expected wait is shorter than the cost of a context switch.
hint: What does putting a thread to sleep actually cost?

body: What is priority inversion?

options.body: A high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task that cannot run
The scheduler assigning priorities in the wrong order
options.whyWrong: Priority assignment is a policy question, not this failure mode.

options.body: A task raising its own priority
options.whyWrong: Self-elevation is a mechanism, not the problem.

options.body: Two tasks with equal priority alternating
options.whyWrong: Equal-priority round-robin is normal operation.

explanation: A medium-priority task can preempt the low-priority lock holder, so the high-priority task is blocked indefinitely. Priority inheritance — temporarily raising the holder’s priority — is the standard fix, and this bug famously afflicted the Mars Pathfinder.
concept: A lock can invert the priority order the scheduler is trying to enforce.
hint: What stops the low-priority holder from finishing?

body: What does "virtual memory" allow beyond isolation?

options.body: A process to use more memory than is physically installed
Programs to run without an operating system
options.whyWrong: Virtual memory is provided by the OS, not a replacement for it.

options.body: Memory access to become faster than physical RAM
options.whyWrong: Translation adds overhead; it does not make memory faster.

options.body: Processes to share every page by default
options.whyWrong: Sharing is possible but is not the default.

explanation: Pages not currently needed can live on disk and be brought in on demand, so the address space can exceed physical memory. The cost is a page fault when an absent page is touched, and thrashing when the working set no longer fits.
concept: Demand paging trades disk latency for a larger apparent address space.
hint: Where do pages live when they are not in RAM?

body: What is the difference between internal and external fragmentation?

options.body: Internal is unused space inside an allocated block; external is unusable gaps between blocks
Internal happens in RAM, external on disk
options.whyWrong: Both occur in either medium.

options.body: Internal affects the kernel, external affects user processes
options.whyWrong: Both affect any allocator.

options.body: They are two names for the same thing
options.whyWrong: They have different causes and different remedies.

explanation: Fixed-size allocation such as paging causes internal fragmentation — the last page is partly wasted. Variable-size allocation causes external fragmentation, where free memory exists but not contiguously. Paging trades the second for the first.
concept: Fixed-size blocks waste inside; variable-size blocks waste between.
hint: Which kind does paging deliberately accept?

body: What happens on a system call?

options.body: The CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to a fixed handler

options.whyWrong: Only fork and its relatives create processes; most system calls do not.
Termination is one specific call, not what system calls do generally.

options.body: The scheduler always runs a different process
options.whyWrong: A system call may block, but many return directly to the caller.

explanation: User code cannot touch hardware directly, so it raises a trap that transfers control to a predetermined kernel entry point with elevated privilege. The kernel validates the arguments — never trusting a user pointer — and returns to user mode afterwards.
concept: A system call is a controlled, one-way door into privileged code.
hint: Why can user code not simply jump into the kernel?

body: In the producer-consumer problem, what does a bounded buffer require?

options.body: Synchronisation for both "buffer full" and "buffer empty" conditions
Only a lock around the buffer
options.whyWrong: A lock alone gives mutual exclusion but no way to wait for space or for data.
Two counting semaphores plus a mutex are needed for the full and empty conditions.

options.body: No synchronisation if the buffer is large enough
options.whyWrong: Size only delays the problem; the race remains.

explanation: The producer must block when the buffer is full and the consumer when it is empty, which needs two counting semaphores plus mutual exclusion on the buffer itself. Handling only one direction is the classic incomplete solution.
concept: Bounded buffers need both mutual exclusion and condition synchronisation.
hint: What should the producer do when there is no space?

body: What is a zombie process?

options.body: A finished process whose exit status has not yet been collected by its parent
A process consuming all the CPU
options.whyWrong: That is a runaway process, not a zombie.
That is an orphan, which init adopts.

options.body: A process stuck waiting on I/O
options.whyWrong: That is simply a blocked process.

explanation: A terminated child stays in the process table until the parent calls wait to read its status. It uses no CPU or memory beyond that entry, but a parent that never reaps its children can exhaust the table — which is why long-running daemons handle SIGCHLD.
concept: A zombie is bookkeeping waiting to be collected, not a running process.
hint: What is the parent supposed to do after a child exits?

body: What does the three-way handshake establish?

options.body: Initial sequence numbers and agreement to open a connection in both directions
The encryption keys for the session
options.whyWrong: TLS negotiates keys after the TCP connection is already open.

options.body: The route the packets will take
options.whyWrong: Routing is decided hop by hop by the network layer.
Bandwidth is discovered by congestion control over time.

explanation: SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK let each side announce its starting sequence number and confirm the other side received it. Random initial sequence numbers also make blind connection spoofing much harder.
concept: TCP’s reliability rests on sequence numbers, which the handshake bootstraps.
hint: What does each side need to know before it can detect a lost byte?

body: Why is UDP preferred for live video calls?

options.body: A retransmitted frame would arrive too late to be useful

options.whyWrong: UDP provides no encryption; that comes from a layer above.
UDP guarantees neither ordering nor delivery.

options.body: UDP has a larger payload limit
options.whyWrong: Payload limits are governed by the path MTU, not the transport choice.

explanation: In real-time media, latency matters more than completeness — a frame that arrives after its moment is useless, and TCP’s retransmission plus head-of-line blocking would stall everything behind it. Applications add their own concealment for lost packets.
concept: Choose the transport by whether late data is still valuable.
hint: What would you do with a video frame that arrives a second late?

body: What does DNS do?

options.body: Resolves domain names to IP addresses
Encrypts traffic between browser and server
options.whyWrong: That is TLS.
Routing is the job of IP and routing protocols.

options.body: Assigns IP addresses to devices on a LAN
options.whyWrong: That is DHCP.

explanation: DNS is a distributed hierarchy from root to TLD to authoritative servers, with caching at every level to keep lookups fast. It is also why a stale cached record can send traffic to an old server after a migration.
concept: DNS is a lookup layer, and its caching is both its strength and its trap.
hint: What has to happen before your browser can open a TCP connection?

body: What is the difference between HTTP status 401 and 403?

options.body: 401 means not authenticated; 403 means authenticated but not permitted
401 is a client error and 403 a server error
options.whyWrong: Both are client errors in the 4xx range.

options.body: 403 means the resource does not exist
options.whyWrong: That is 404.
They convey different situations, and the difference guides what the client should do next.

explanation: 401 invites the client to authenticate and should carry a WWW-Authenticate header; 403 says the identity is known and still not allowed, so retrying with the same credentials is pointless. Some APIs deliberately return 404 instead of 403 to avoid revealing that a resource exists.
concept: The status code tells the client whether retrying with credentials could help.
hint: Would logging in fix the problem?

body: What is the purpose of an ARP request?

options.body: To find the MAC address matching a known IP address on the local network
To find the IP address for a domain name
options.whyWrong: That is DNS.

options.body: To assign an IP address to a new device
options.whyWrong: That is DHCP.

options.body: To test whether a host is reachable
options.whyWrong: That is ping, using ICMP.

explanation: Ethernet frames are addressed by MAC, so a host with an IP destination on its own subnet must first discover the hardware address. ARP broadcasts the question to the local segment; the trust it places in any reply is what makes ARP spoofing possible.
concept: IP addresses route between networks; MAC addresses deliver within one.
hint: What address does an Ethernet frame actually carry?

body: What does a subnet mask determine?

options.body: Which part of an IP address identifies the network and which the host
The maximum speed of the network
options.whyWrong: Speed is a property of the physical link.
The mask says nothing about protocols.
The gateway is configured separately.

explanation: The mask marks the leading network bits, so a host can tell whether a destination is on its own subnet — deliverable directly — or must be sent to the gateway. A wrong mask makes local hosts unreachable while the internet still works, or the reverse.
concept: The mask answers one question: is this destination local or remote?
hint: How does a host decide whether to use the gateway?

body: Why does TCP use a sliding window?

options.body: To send several segments before waiting for acknowledgement, while bounding the receiver’s load

options.whyWrong: Windowing has nothing to do with encryption.

options.body: To split large files into packets
options.whyWrong: Segmentation is separate from flow control.
Routes are not TCP’s concern.

explanation: Stop-and-wait would cap throughput at one segment per round trip. The window allows several segments in flight, and the receiver advertises its size so a fast sender cannot overwhelm a slow receiver. Congestion control adds a second, network-driven limit.
concept: Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network.
hint: What limits throughput if you must wait for every ACK?

body: What layer of the OSI model does a router primarily operate at?

options.whyWrong: Switches operate at the data-link layer using MAC addresses.
Transport is TCP and UDP, above routing.
Application-layer devices are proxies and gateways.

explanation: A router forwards packets between networks using IP addresses, which is layer 3. A switch works within one network using MAC addresses at layer 2 — the distinction that decides which device you need.
concept: Layer 2 delivers within a network; layer 3 moves between networks.
hint: Which address does the device examine to make its decision?

body: What problem does HTTPS solve that HTTP does not?

options.body: Confidentiality and integrity of traffic, plus server identity

options.whyWrong: HTTPS adds a handshake, though HTTP/2 over TLS often ends up faster overall.
Compression is negotiated independently of TLS.
Delivery guarantees come from TCP beneath it.

explanation: TLS encrypts the traffic, detects tampering, and authenticates the server via a certificate chain. Without it, anyone on the path can read and modify the exchange — which is why certificate warnings should never be clicked past.
concept: TLS provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication — three properties, not one.
hint: What can someone on the same Wi-Fi see over plain HTTP?

body: What is the difference between a switch and a hub?

options.body: A switch forwards a frame only to the port with the destination MAC; a hub repeats it everywhere

options.whyWrong: Repeating to every port wastes bandwidth and causes collisions.

options.body: A switch works only with fibre
options.whyWrong: Both work over copper or fibre.
A hub is a layer-1 repeater with no addressing at all.

explanation: A switch learns which MAC lives behind each port and forwards selectively, so several conversations proceed at once. A hub is an electrical repeater, putting every device in one collision domain — which is why hubs disappeared.
concept: Selective forwarding is what lets a switch give each port its own bandwidth.
hint: What happens when two devices transmit at once on a hub?

body: What does a load balancer’s health check accomplish?

options.body: It stops traffic being sent to instances that are failing
It measures CPU usage for billing
options.whyWrong: Billing is unrelated to health checking.

options.body: It encrypts traffic to the backend
options.whyWrong: Encryption is a separate configuration.
Caching is a distinct function.

explanation: The balancer polls each backend and removes failing ones from rotation, so users are not routed to a broken instance. A check that only tests whether the port is open will happily keep sending traffic to a process that has stopped serving correctly.
concept: A health check is only as good as the thing it actually tests.
hint: Is an open port the same as a working service?

body: Why is idempotency important when a client retries a request over an unreliable network?

options.body: The client cannot tell whether a timed-out request was processed, so a repeat must be safe
Retries are always faster than the original
options.whyWrong: Speed is not the concern.

options.body: Idempotent requests skip the network stack
options.whyWrong: Every request goes over the network.
Any request can time out.

explanation: A timeout means the response was lost, which may or may not mean the request was. If the operation is idempotent, retrying is harmless. If not — a payment, say — you need an idempotency key so the server recognises the duplicate.
concept: Design for the case where the client does not know what happened.
hint: What might have happened to a request that timed out?

body: In the edit-distance DP between two strings, what does dp[i][j] hold?

options.body: The minimum edits to turn the first i characters of one string into the first j of the other
Whether the two prefixes are equal
options.whyWrong: A boolean cannot express a minimum cost.

options.body: The length of their longest common subsequence
options.whyWrong: That is a different recurrence with a different meaning.
Simple mismatch counting only works for equal-length strings and ignores insertions.

explanation: When the characters match the cost carries over from dp[i−1][j−1]; otherwise it is one plus the cheapest of insert, delete or replace. Defining the state over prefix pairs is what makes the recurrence close.
concept: Most two-string DP problems index by a prefix of each string.
hint: What are the two things a subproblem depends on here?

body: The longest palindromic substring DP fills its table in what order, and why?

options.body: By increasing substring length, because a longer substring depends on a shorter inner one
Left to right by starting index
options.whyWrong: A left-to-right sweep can reach a cell before the inner substring it needs is computed.

options.body: In any order, since the cells are independent
options.whyWrong: The cells are not independent — that dependence is what makes it DP.

options.body: From the end backwards by character
options.whyWrong: Character order alone does not respect the dependency.

explanation: dp[i][j] is true when the characters at i and j match and dp[i+1][j−1] is already true. That inner substring is two characters shorter, so filling by increasing length guarantees it is ready when needed.
concept: Fill order must follow the dependency direction of the recurrence.
hint: Which cell must already be computed before dp[i][j] can be?
